The self-inductance with a magnetic core of relative permeability \( \mu_r \) is:
\[ L = \mu_r L_0 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute into the expression:
\[ L = 600 \times (1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}) = 900 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H} = 0.90\text{ H} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying: \( 600 \times 1.5\text{ mH} = 900\text{ mH} = 0.90\text{ H} \). The new self-inductance is \( 0.90\text{ H} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q26 - Electromotive force in loop inside powered solenoid

questiontext.text: A long solenoid with \( 15\text{ turns per cm} \) has a small circular wire loop of area \( 2.0\text{ cm}^2 \) placed inside near its centre with its plane perpendicular to the solenoid's axis. If the current carried by the solenoid increases steadily from \( 2.0\text{ A} \) to \( 4.0\text{ A} \) in \( 0.10\text{ s} \), what is the magnitude of the induced electromotive force in the loop? (Take \( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A} \) and \( \pi \approx 3.142 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Turn density: \( n = 15\text{ cm}^{-1} = 1500\text{ m}^{-1} \).
Loop area: \( A = 2.0\text{ cm}^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 \).
Current change: \( \Delta I = 4.0\text{ A} - 2.0\text{ A} = 2.0\text{ A} \).
Time interval: \( \Delta t = 0.10\text{ s} \).
Plane of loop is normal to axis, so \( \theta = 0^\circ \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The solenoid is long, so the magnetic field inside is uniform: \( B = \mu_0 n I \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Rate of change of magnetic field: \( \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mu_0 n \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \).
Induced emf in the loop: \( \varepsilon = A \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = A \mu_0 n \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = \frac{2.0\text{ A}}{0.10\text{ s}} = 20\text{ A s}^{-1} \).
Substitute into formula:
\[ \varepsilon = (2.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2) \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}) \times (1500\text{ m}^{-1}) \times (20\text{ A s}^{-1}) \]
\[ \varepsilon = (2.0 \times 10^{-4}) \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 30000 \]
\[ \varepsilon = 24\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ V} \approx 24 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-7}\text{ V} \approx 7.54 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V} \approx 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Evaluating: \( 24\pi \times 10^{-7} \approx 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V} \). The magnitude of the induced electromotive force is \( 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q27 - Induced electromotive force exiting along longer edge

questiontext.text: A rectangular wire loop of sides \( 8.0\text{ cm} \) and \( 2.0\text{ cm} \) with a small cut is pulled out of a region of uniform magnetic field \( B = 0.30\text{ T} \) (normal to the loop) at a constant velocity of \( 1.0\text{ cm s}^{-1} \). When the loop is moved normal to its longer side (length \( 8.0\text{ cm} \)), what is the induced electromotive force across the cut and for how long does this voltage persist?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Longer side: \( a = 8.0\text{ cm} = 0.080\text{ m} \).
Shorter side: \( b = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.020\text{ m} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.30\text{ T} \).
Speed: \( v = 1.0\text{ cm s}^{-1} = 0.010\text{ m s}^{-1} \).
The motion is normal to the longer side, meaning the active cutting edge has length \( l = a = 8.0\text{ cm} = 0.080\text{ m} \), and the distance traversed to exit the field is the shorter side \( b = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.020\text{ m} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field is spatially uniform inside the boundary and zero outside.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Induced motional emf: \( \varepsilon = B l v \).
Duration of induced voltage: \( \Delta t = \frac{b}{v} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate induced emf:
\[ \varepsilon = (0.30\text{ T}) \times (0.080\text{ m}) \times (0.010\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 2.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V} \]
Calculate duration:
\[ \Delta t = \frac{2.0\text{ cm}}{1.0\text{ cm s}^{-1}} = 2.0\text{ s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Moving normal to the longer side produces an induced emf of \( 2.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ V} \) lasting for \( 2.0\text{ s} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q28 - Magnetic retarding force and electrical power dissipation

questiontext.text: A conducting rod of length \( 0.50\text{ m} \) and resistance \( 0.20\ \Omega \) slides with a constant velocity of \( 6.0\text{ m s}^{-1} \) on two frictionless horizontal rails. The rails are connected across an external resistor of \( 1.0\ \Omega \). A uniform magnetic field of \( 1.2\text{ T} \) is directed vertically downwards. What external mechanical force is required to sustain this motion, and what is the electrical power dissipated as heat in the circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of rod: \( l = 0.50\text{ m} \).
Internal resistance of rod: \( r = 0.20\ \Omega \).
External resistor: \( R = 1.0\ \Omega \).
Total resistance: \( R_{\text{tot}} = R + r = 1.0 + 0.20 = 1.2\ \Omega \).
Speed: \( v = 6.0\text{ m s}^{-1} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 1.2\text{ T} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Rails have negligible resistance, and mechanical friction is zero.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Motional emf: \( \varepsilon = B l v \).
Induced current: \( I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R_{\text{tot}}} = \frac{B l v}{R_{\text{tot}}} \).
Magnetic retarding force: \( F = I l B = \frac{B^2 l^2 v}{R_{\text{tot}}} \).
Power dissipated: \( P = F v = I^2 R_{\text{tot}} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate induced emf:
\[ \varepsilon = (1.2\text{ T}) \times (0.50\text{ m}) \times (6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 3.6\text{ V} \]
Calculate induced current:
\[ I = \frac{3.6\text{ V}}{1.2\ \Omega} = 3.0\text{ A} \]
Calculate external mechanical force:
\[ F = I l B = (3.0\text{ A}) \times (0.50\text{ m}) \times (1.2\text{ T}) = 1.8\text{ N} \]
Calculate power dissipated:
\[ P = F v = (1.8\text{ N}) \times (6.0\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 10.8\text{ W} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verify using Joule heat: \( I^2 R_{\text{tot}} = (3.0)^2 \times 1.2 = 9.0 \times 1.2 = 10.8\text{ W} \). The required force is \( 1.8\text{ N} \) and the dissipated power is \( 10.8\text{ W} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q29 - Electromotive force induced in rotating quadrant frame

questiontext.text: A conducting wire frame shaped as a circular sector of radius \( R = 0.40\text{ m} \) with central angle \( 90^\circ \) (a quadrant) rotates with uniform angular velocity \( \omega = 50\text{ rad s}^{-1} \) in its plane about its central apex. A uniform magnetic field \( B = 1.5\text{ T} \) is directed perpendicular to the plane of rotation. What is the magnitude of the electromotive force induced across the two radial edges while the quadrant is entering the magnetic field region?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius: \( R = 0.40\text{ m} \).
Angular velocity: \( \omega = 50\text{ rad s}^{-1} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 1.5\text{ T} \) perpendicular to the sector plane.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The apex is stationary and acts as the center of rotation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Area swept per unit time is \( \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{2} R^2 \omega \).
The induced electromotive force across the radial arms is:
\[ \varepsilon = B \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( R^2 = (0.40\text{ m})^2 = 0.16\text{ m}^2 \).
Substitute into formula:
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times (1.5\text{ T}) \times (50\text{ rad s}^{-1}) \times (0.16\text{ m}^2) \]
\[ \varepsilon = 0.75 \times 50 \times 0.16 = 37.5 \times 0.16 = 6.0\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking calculation: \( 0.5 \times 1.5 \times 50 \times 0.16 = 6.0\text{ V} \). The induced electromotive force is \( 6.0\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q30 - Induced electric field inside varying magnetic cylinder

questiontext.text: A long cylindrical region of radius \( R = 0.20\text{ m} \) contains a spatially uniform magnetic field directed parallel to its axis. The magnetic field increases at a constant rate of \( \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.50\text{ T s}^{-1} \). What is the magnitude of the induced non-conservative electric field at a radial distance of \( r = 0.10\text{ m} \) from the central axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Cylinder radius: \( R = 0.20\text{ m} \).
Rate of magnetic field increase: \( \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.50\text{ T s}^{-1} \).
Observation distance: \( r = 0.10\text{ m} \) (inside the cylinder, \( r < R \)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Cylindrical symmetry dictates that the electric field lines are concentric circles centered on the cylindrical axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Faraday's law in integral form:
\[ \oint \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \]
For \( r < R \): \( E(2\pi r) = (\pi r^2) \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} \implies E = \frac{1}{2} r \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[ E = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.10\text{ m}) \times (0.50\text{ T s}^{-1}) = 0.050 \times 0.50 = 0.025\text{ V m}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \( \text{m}\cdot(\text{T/s}) = \text{m}\cdot(\text{V}\cdot\text{s/m}^2)/\text{s} = \text{V/m} \). The magnitude of the induced electric field is \( 0.025\text{ V m}^{-1} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q31 - Equivalent inductance of series opposing coupled coils

questiontext.text: Two coils with self-inductances \( L_1 = 8.0\text{ mH} \) and \( L_2 = 18\text{ mH} \) have a coupling coefficient of \( k = 0.50 \). If they are connected in series such that their magnetic fluxes oppose each other, what is the effective equivalent self-inductance of the combination?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Self-inductances: \( L_1 = 8.0\text{ mH} \), \( L_2 = 18\text{ mH} \).
Coupling coefficient: \( k = 0.50 \).
Connection: Series opposing.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Linear magnetic medium with constant mutual inductance.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Mutual inductance is given by:
\[ M = k \sqrt{L_1 L_2} \]
For two coils connected in series opposing, the equivalent inductance is:
\[ L_{\text{eq}} = L_1 + L_2 - 2M \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \( \sqrt{L_1 L_2} = \sqrt{8.0 \times 18} = \sqrt{144} = 12\text{ mH} \).
Calculate mutual inductance:
\[ M = 0.50 \times 12\text{ mH} = 6.0\text{ mH} \]
Calculate equivalent inductance:
\[ L_{\text{eq}} = 8.0\text{ mH} + 18\text{ mH} - 2(6.0\text{ mH}) = 26\text{ mH} - 12\text{ mH} = 14\text{ mH} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Evaluating: \( 26 - 12 = 14\text{ mH} \). The equivalent self-inductance is \( 14\text{ mH} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q32 - Induced current from quadratic magnetic field variation

questiontext.text: A planar conducting loop of surface area \( A = 0.050\text{ m}^2 \) and resistance \( R = 1.5\ \Omega \) is held perpendicular to a magnetic field whose magnitude varies with time according to \( B(t) = 2.0\, t^2 + 3.0\, t \) (where \( B \) is in teslas and \( t \) is in seconds). What is the magnitude of the induced electric current in the loop at time \( t = 2.0\text{ s} \)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Area: \( A = 0.050\text{ m}^2 \).
Resistance: \( R = 1.5\ \Omega \).
Magnetic field function: \( B(t) = 2.0\, t^2 + 3.0\, t \).
Time instant: \( t = 2.0\text{ s} \).
Plane of loop is perpendicular to field, so \( \theta = 0^\circ \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Self-inductance of the loop is negligible.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Rate of change of magnetic field: \( \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2.0\, t^2 + 3.0\, t) = 4.0\, t + 3.0 \).
Induced emf: \( \varepsilon = A \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} \).
Induced current: \( I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At \( t = 2.0\text{ s} \):
\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = (4.0 \times 2.0) + 3.0 = 8.0 + 3.0 = 11\text{ T s}^{-1} \]
Calculate induced emf:
\[ \varepsilon = (0.050\text{ m}^2) \times (11\text{ T s}^{-1}) = 0.55\text{ V} \]
Calculate induced current:
\[ I = \frac{0.55\text{ V}}{1.5\ \Omega} = \frac{11}{30}\text{ A} \approx 0.367\text{ A} \approx 0.37\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking calculation: \( 0.55 / 1.5 \approx 0.37\text{ A} \). The induced electric current is \( 0.37\text{ A} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q33 - Terminal velocity calculation of vertically falling rail

questiontext.text: A horizontal conducting rod of mass \( m = 20\text{ g} \), length \( l = 0.40\text{ m} \), and negligible internal resistance slides down two vertical parallel frictionless conducting rails separated by distance \( l \). The rails are connected at the top by a resistor of resistance \( R = 0.80\ \Omega \). A uniform horizontal magnetic field of \( B = 0.50\text{ T} \) is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Taking \( g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \), what is the terminal velocity reached by the rod?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of rod: \( m = 20\text{ g} = 0.020\text{ kg} \).
Length of rod: \( l = 0.40\text{ m} \).
Top resistor: \( R = 0.80\ \Omega \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.50\text{ T} \).
Acceleration due to gravity: \( g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Friction between rod and rails is zero. The rails remain vertical and parallel.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Motional emf: \( \varepsilon = B l v \).
Upward magnetic force: \( F_{\text{mag}} = \frac{B^2 l^2 v}{R} \).
At terminal velocity \( v_t \), the downward gravitational force equals the upward magnetic retarding force:
\[ m g = \frac{B^2 l^2 v_t}{R} \implies v_t = \frac{m g R}{B^2 l^2} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Numerator: \( m g R = (0.020\text{ kg}) \times (9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}) \times (0.80\ \Omega) = 0.196 \times 0.80 = 0.1568\text{ N}\cdot\Omega \).
Denominator: \( B^2 l^2 = (0.50\text{ T})^2 \times (0.40\text{ m})^2 = 0.25 \times 0.16 = 0.040\text{ T}^2\text{m}^2 \).
Calculate terminal velocity:
\[ v_t = \frac{0.1568}{0.040} = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-1} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking dimensions: \( \text{N}\cdot\Omega / (\text{T}^2\text{m}^2) = \text{m s}^{-1} \). The terminal velocity reached is \( 3.92\text{ m s}^{-1} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q34 - Mutual inductance between long wire and adjacent loop

questiontext.text: A long straight wire carrying electric current lies coplanar with a rectangular loop of width \( a = 10\text{ cm} \) (perpendicular to the wire) and length \( b = 20\text{ cm} \) (parallel to the wire). The nearest side of the loop is at a distance \( d = 10\text{ cm} \) from the straight wire. What is the mutual inductance between the wire and the loop? (Take \( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A} \) and \( \ln 2 \approx 0.693 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Width of loop: \( a = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m} \).
Length of loop: \( b = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m} \).
Distance of closest edge: \( d = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m} \).
Distance of farthest edge: \( d + a = 0.10 + 0.10 = 0.20\text{ m} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The straight wire is assumed infinitely long, and the loop is coplanar with it.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic field at distance \( x \) from the straight wire carrying current \( I \) is \( B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi x} \).
Flux through loop: \( \Phi = \int_d^{d+a} B(x) b \,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\mu_0 I b}{2\pi} \ln\left(1 + \frac{a}{d}\right) \).
Mutual inductance: \( M = \frac{\Phi}{I} = \frac{\mu_0 b}{2\pi} \ln\left(1 + \frac{a}{d}\right) \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Ratio: \( 1 + \frac{a}{d} = 1 + \frac{0.10}{0.10} = 2.0 \).
Logarithm: \( \ln(2.0) \approx 0.693 \).
Coefficient: \( \frac{\mu_0 b}{2\pi} = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 0.20}{2\pi} = 4.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H} \).
Calculate \( M \):
\[ M = (4.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H}) \times 0.693 = 2.772 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H} \approx 2.77 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking calculation: \( 4 \times 0.693 \times 10^{-8} = 2.772 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H} \). The mutual inductance is \( 2.77 \times 10^{-8}\text{ H} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q35 - Average mechanical power driving loaded generator armature

questiontext.text: An AC generator has an armature coil of \( 200 \) turns, each of area \( 0.050\text{ m}^2 \), rotating at a constant angular frequency of \( 100\text{ rad s}^{-1} \) in a uniform magnetic field of \( 0.10\text{ T} \). The coil is connected to an external load resistor of total circuit resistance \( 50\ \Omega \). Neglecting mechanical friction, what is the time-averaged mechanical power required to drive the generator?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Turns: \( N = 200 \).
Area: \( A = 0.050\text{ m}^2 \).
Angular speed: \( \omega = 100\text{ rad s}^{-1} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.10\text{ T} \).
Total resistance: \( R = 50\ \Omega \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Mechanical power input equals the electrical power dissipated in the load resistor in steady state.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Peak electromotive force: \( \varepsilon_0 = N B A \\omega \).
Time-averaged power in a purely resistive AC circuit:
\[ P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\varepsilon_0^2}{2 R} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate peak emf:
\[ \varepsilon_0 = 200 \times (0.10\text{ T}) \times (0.050\text{ m}^2) \times (100\text{ rad s}^{-1}) \]
\[ \varepsilon_0 = 20 \times 5.0 = 100\text{ V} \]
Calculate \( \varepsilon_0^2 = (100\text{ V})^2 = 10000\text{ V}^2 \).
Calculate average power:
\[ P_{\text{avg}} = \frac{10000\text{ V}^2}{2 \times 50\ \Omega} = \frac{10000}{100} = 100\text{ W} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \( \text{V}^2/\\Omega = \text{W} \). The time-averaged mechanical power required is \( 100\text{ W} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_NUMERICAL_Q36 - Energy stored during current growth in inductor

questiontext.text: A \( 12\text{ V} \) ideal DC battery is connected in series with a pure inductor of self-inductance \( 0.20\text{ H} \) and a resistor of resistance \( 6.0\ \Omega \). During the establishment of the steady-state electric current, what is the magnetic energy stored in the inductor and the total work done by the battery?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Battery emf: \( \varepsilon = 12\text{ V} \).
Inductance: \( L = 0.20\text{ H} \).
Resistance: \( R = 6.0\ \Omega \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Current starts from zero at \( t = 0 \) and reaches steady-state value \( I_0 \) after several time constants.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Steady-state current: \( I_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} \).
Magnetic energy stored in inductor: \( U_B = \frac{1}{2} L I_0^2 \).
Total work done by the battery during current rise: \( W_b = L I_0^2 = 2 U_B \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate steady current:
\[ I_0 = \frac{12\text{ V}}{6.0\ \Omega} = 2.0\text{ A} \]
Calculate \( I_0^2 = (2.0\text{ A})^2 = 4.0\text{ A}^2 \).
Calculate magnetic energy stored in inductor:
\[ U_B = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.20\text{ H}) \times (4.0\text{ A}^2) = 0.10 \times 4.0 = 0.40\text{ J} \]
Calculate total work done by battery:
\[ W_b = L I_0^2 = (0.20\text{ H}) \times (4.0\text{ A}^2) = 0.80\text{ J} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Heat dissipated in the resistor is \( H = W_b - U_B = 0.80\text{ J} - 0.40\text{ J} = 0.40\text{ J} \). The stored magnetic energy is \( 0.40\text{ J} \) and the total work done by the battery is \( 0.80\text{ J} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Logical sequence of electromagnetic induction in a coil

questiontext.text:
Consider Faraday's experiment where the North pole of a bar magnet is pushed along the axis towards a stationary closed conducting coil connected to a sensitive galvanometer. Arrange the following events in the correct chronological and physical sequence from the initiation of motion to the detection of current:

  1. An induced current circulates in the coil in a direction such that its magnetic dipole opposes the approach of the North pole.
  2. The North pole of the bar magnet is moved towards the face of the stationary coil with a certain velocity.
  3. The pointer of the galvanometer deflects from zero, confirming the flow of induced current.
  4. An induced electromotive force is generated across the turns of the closed coil in accordance with Faraday's law.
  5. The density of magnetic field lines passing through the area bounded by the coil increases, causing a time-varying magnetic flux.

Choose the correct sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electromagnetic induction is governed by Faraday's and Lenz's laws. A mechanical change in the relative position of a magnet and a coil alters the magnetic flux through the coil, which sequentially produces an induced electromotive force, drives an induced current, and causes a galvanometer deflection.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sequential Stages
1. First, external work begins when the North pole of the bar magnet is moved towards the face of the stationary coil (Stage II).
2. As the magnet draws nearer, the magnetic field lines penetrating the coil become denser, which increases the magnetic flux linked with the coil over time (Stage V).
3. By Faraday's law of induction, this non-zero time rate of change of magnetic flux induces an electromotive force across the coil (Stage IV).
4. In a closed circuit of finite resistance, this induced electromotive force drives an induced electric current that circulates counter-clockwise (viewed from the magnet's side) to produce a North pole that repels the approaching magnet, complying with Lenz's law (Stage I).
5. Finally, the circulating current flows through the external galvanometer, causing its pointer to deflect and visibly indicate the current (Stage III).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological and physical sequence of events is II → V → IV → I → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequential stages of armature rotation in AC generator

questiontext.text:
In an alternating current (AC) generator, a flat rectangular armature coil rotates with a constant angular frequency \(\omega\) in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\). At time \(t = 0\), the plane of the armature coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field lines. Arrange the following states of the armature coil and its induced electromotive force (emf) \(\varepsilon\) in the correct chronological order as the coil completes one full rotation from \(t = 0\) to \(t = T\):

  1. The armature coil rotates through an angle of \(270^\circ\) (at \(t = 3T/4\)), where its plane is parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\) and the induced emf attains its negative peak value \(-\varepsilon_0\).
  2. The armature coil rotates through an angle of \(90^\circ\) (at \(t = T/4\)), where its plane is parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\) and the induced emf attains its positive peak value \(+\varepsilon_0\).
  3. The plane of the armature coil is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\) at \(t = 0\), where the linked magnetic flux is maximum and the induced emf is zero (\(\varepsilon = 0\)).
  4. The armature coil completes a full rotation of \(360^\circ\) (at \(t = T\)), returning to its initial orientation with zero induced emf (\(\varepsilon = 0\)).
  5. The armature coil rotates through an angle of \(180^\circ\) (at \(t = T/2\)), where its plane is again perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\) and the induced emf momentarily drops to zero (\(\varepsilon = 0\)).

Choose the correct sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an AC generator, the magnetic flux through a coil of \(N\) turns and area \(A\) at any angle \(\theta = \omega t\) is given by \(\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = B A \cos(\omega t)\). By Faraday's law, the instantaneous induced electromotive force is \(\varepsilon(t) = -N\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = N B A \omega \sin(\omega t) = \varepsilon_0 \sin(\omega t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Sequential Stages
1. At \(t = 0\) (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)): The plane of the armature is perpendicular to the field. Here \(\cos(0^\circ) = 1\) (maximum flux) and \(\sin(0^\circ) = 0\), so the induced electromotive force is zero (Stage III).
2. At \(t = T/4\) (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)): The plane of the armature is parallel to the field. Flux is zero, but the rate of change of flux is maximum with \(\sin(90^\circ) = 1\), giving the positive peak electromotive force \(\varepsilon = +\varepsilon_0\) (Stage II).
3. At \(t = T/2\) (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)): The plane of the armature is perpendicular to the field again with reversed face orientation. Flux reaches an extreme in reverse, while \(\sin(180^\circ) = 0\), causing the induced electromotive force to pass through zero (Stage V).
4. At \(t = 3T/4\) (\(\theta = 270^\circ\)): The plane of the armature is again parallel to the field. Here \(\sin(270^\circ) = -1\), producing the negative peak electromotive force \(\varepsilon = -\varepsilon_0\) (Stage I).
5. At \(t = T\) (\(\theta = 360^\circ\)): The armature completes a full cycle of rotation, returning to the starting configuration where \(\sin(360^\circ) = 0\) and the induced electromotive force returns to zero (Stage IV).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of stages during one complete rotation is III → II → V → I → IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Microscopic mechanism of motional emf generation

questiontext.text:
Consider a conducting rod of length \(l\) placed across two parallel, frictionless conducting rails in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) directed perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The rails are connected at one end to form a complete circuit. Arrange the following steps in the correct causal and physical sequence explaining the generation of motional electromotive force and steady induced current when the rod is moved with constant velocity \(\mathbf{v}\):

  1. An internal electrostatic electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) builds up along the rod, exerting an electrostatic force \(\mathbf{F}_e = -e\mathbf{E}\) that opposes further magnetic deflection of electrons.
  2. Free conduction electrons inside the moving rod experience a magnetic Lorentz force \(\mathbf{F}_m = -e(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\) directed along the rod.
  3. A dynamic equilibrium is established where the magnetic Lorentz force balances the electrostatic force, setting up a steady potential difference (motional emf) \(\varepsilon = B l v\) across the rod.
  4. The external agent moves the conducting rod with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) perpendicular to the magnetic field.
  5. Displaced conduction electrons accumulate at one terminal of the rod, leaving a deficit of negative charge (net positive charge) at the opposite terminal.

Choose the correct sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Motional electromotive force can be explained microscopically by the Lorentz force acting on mobile charge carriers in a moving conductor. Separation of charges gives rise to an opposing electrostatic electric field until a steady-state potential difference is reached.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sequential Stages
1. Initially, the conducting rod is set into motion with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) perpendicular to the magnetic field by an external agent (Stage IV).
2. Conduction electrons, which share the bulk velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) of the rod, experience a transverse magnetic Lorentz force given by \(\mathbf{F}_m = -e(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\) along the rod (Stage II).
3. Driven by this magnetic force, free electrons drift and accumulate at one end of the rod, leaving an excess of unneutralized positive lattice ions at the other end (Stage V).
4. This charge separation creates an electrostatic electric field \(\mathbf{E}\) directed from the positive end to the negative end, which exerts an opposing electrostatic force \(\mathbf{F}_e = -e\mathbf{E}\) on the electrons (Stage I).
5. Accumulation continues until a dynamic equilibrium is reached where \(eE = evB\), maintaining a steady induced electromotive force \(\varepsilon = E l = B l v\) that drives current through the closed loop (Stage III).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical and physical sequence is IV → II → V → I → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Growth of current and energy storage in an inductor

questiontext.text:
An external voltage source is connected across an inductor of self-inductance \(L\) and negligible resistance to establish a steady current \(I\). Arrange the following physical steps in the correct logical and chronological sequence describing the build-up of current and the storage of magnetic potential energy in the inductor:

  1. The external source does work against the induced back emf at the instantaneous rate \(\frac{\mathrm{d}W}{\mathrm{d}t} = |\varepsilon| i = L i \frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\).
  2. A time-varying current begins to grow in the coil, establishing a time-dependent rate of change of current \(\frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} > 0\).
  3. The total work done in establishing the final current \(I\) is integrated as \(W = \int_0^I L i \,\mathrm{d}i = \frac{1}{2} L I^2\), which is stored as magnetic potential energy.
  4. The changing current produces a changing magnetic flux linkage \(N\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = L i\) through the turns of the inductor.
  5. By Faraday's and Lenz's laws, a self-induced back electromotive force \(\varepsilon = -L\frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is generated that opposes the further growth of current.

Choose the correct sequence:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Self-inductance represents electrical inertia. When current is established in an inductor, energy must be expended by the external source to do work against the self-induced back electromotive force. This mechanical/electrical work is conserved and stored as magnetic field energy.

Step 2: Evaluation of Sequential Stages
1. When the circuit is closed, current starts to rise from zero, creating a non-zero rate of growth \(\frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} > 0\) (Stage II).
2. As current \(i\) increases, the magnetic field and the resulting total magnetic flux linkage \(N\Phi_{\mathrm{B}} = L i\) through the coil turns increase proportionally (Stage IV).
3. According to Faraday's law of induction and Lenz's law, this changing flux linkage induces an opposing back electromotive force \(\varepsilon = -L\frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\) (Stage V).
4. To maintain current growth against this opposing electromotive force, the external electrical source must supply power and do work at the instantaneous rate \(\frac{\mathrm{d}W}{\mathrm{d}t} = |\varepsilon| i = L i \frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t}\) (Stage I).
5. Integrating this rate of work over the entire growth period from current \(0\) to final current \(I\) yields the total work \(W = \int_0^I L i \,\mathrm{d}i = \frac{1}{2} L I^2\), which is fully stored as magnetic energy in the inductor (Stage III).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence of steps is II → IV → V → I → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q01 - Discovery of electromagnetic induction by pioneer physicists

questiontext.text: The phenomenon in which an electromotive force (emf) and electric current are induced in a closed circuit by a changing magnetic field was conclusively demonstrated around 1830 by which of the following pairs of physicists?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electromagnetic induction is the physical process whereby a time-varying magnetic field or relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field induces an electromotive force (emf) and electric current in a closed loop.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
In the early 1830s, independent experimental investigations carried out by Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in the United States conclusively demonstrated that varying magnetic flux through closed coils generates induced electric currents.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
While Hans Christian Oersted and André-Marie Ampère previously established that steady electric currents create magnetic fields, the reciprocal discovery that changing magnetic fields produce electricity was pioneered by Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The historical discovery of electromagnetic induction is credited to Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q02 - Effect of magnet speed on galvanometer deflection

questiontext.text: In Faraday's experimental arrangement consisting of a stationary conducting coil connected to a sensitive galvanometer, when the North pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards the coil with a higher speed, the galvanometer deflection:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, the magnitude of the induced electromotive force in a circuit is directly proportional to the time rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit, given by \( |\varepsilon| = \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \).

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
When the bar magnet is moved faster towards the coil, the magnetic flux linked with the coil changes by the same total amount in a much shorter time interval \( \Delta t \). Consequently, the rate of change of magnetic flux \( \frac{\Delta \Phi_B}{\Delta t} \) increases.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
A larger induced emf across the fixed coil resistance \( R \) establishes a proportionally larger induced electric current \( I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} \), producing a greater angular deflection of the galvanometer pointer.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Pushing the magnet towards the coil faster increases the magnitude of the galvanometer deflection.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q03 - Definition and standard unit of magnetic flux

questiontext.text: Magnetic flux linked with a flat surface of area vector \( \mathbf{A} \) placed in a uniform magnetic field \( \mathbf{B} \) is defined as \( \Phi_B = \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathbf{A} \). What is the SI unit of magnetic flux?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Magnetic flux is defined mathematically as the scalar dot product of the uniform magnetic field vector \( \mathbf{B} \) and the area vector \( \mathbf{A} \), expressed as \( \Phi_B = B A \cos\theta \).

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
The SI unit of magnetic field \( B \) is tesla (\( \text{T} \)) and the SI unit of area \( A \) is square metre (\( \text{m}^2 \)). Therefore, the unit of magnetic flux is tesla metre squared (\( \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2 \)).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
In the International System of Units (SI), one tesla metre squared is designated by the special name weber (symbol: \( \text{Wb} \)).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The SI unit of magnetic flux is weber (\( \text{Wb} \)) or tesla metre squared (\( \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2 \)).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q04 - Dimensional formula of scalar magnetic flux

questiontext.text: The dimensional formula of magnetic flux \( \Phi_B \) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The physical quantity is magnetic flux \( \Phi_B = B A \cos\theta \), where \( B \) is magnetic field and \( A \) is surface area.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The angle \( \theta \) is dimensionless. The magnetic field \( B \) is evaluated from the magnetic Lorentz force relation \( F = q v B \sin\phi \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[ [B] = \frac{[F]}{[q][v]} = \frac{[\text{M L T}^{-2}]}{[\text{A T}][\text{L T}^{-1}]} = [\text{M T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}] \]
\[ [A] = [\text{L}^2] \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Multiplying the dimensions of magnetic field by the dimensions of area:
\[ [\Phi_B] = [B][A] = [\text{M T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}][\text{L}^2] = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}] \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since work per unit current is energy divided by current, \( [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2}]/[\text{A}] = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}] \), the dimensional formula is \( [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}] \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q05 - Dependence of induced electromotive force on turns

questiontext.text: A closely wound flat coil consists of \( N \) identical turns. If the magnetic flux linked with each turn changes with time at a rate \( \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \), the total induced electromotive force \( \varepsilon \) developed across the coil is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a closely wound coil of \( N \) turns, each individual turn encloses essentially the same cross-sectional area and is linked with the same magnetic flux \( \Phi_B \).

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
The individual turns are electrically connected in series. Therefore, the electromotive forces induced in each turn add up algebraically.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
The total induced electromotive force across the \( N \) turns is given by Faraday's law as \( \varepsilon = -N \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \), showing that the induced emf is directly proportional to the number of turns \( N \).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total induced electromotive force is \( \varepsilon = -N \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q06 - Underlying conservation principle of Lenz law rule

questiontext.text: Lenz's law, which states that the polarity of an induced electromotive force is such that it tends to produce an electric current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it, is a direct consequence of which fundamental principle of physics?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lenz's law provides the direction of induced emf and current in electromagnetic induction, stating that the induced effect always opposes the cause producing it.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
If the induced current were in such a direction as to assist the change in magnetic flux, an approaching bar magnet would be attracted with an ever-increasing acceleration without expenditure of external energy. This self-sustaining acceleration would create kinetic energy and electrical energy from nothing.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
Such a perpetual-motion process is physically impossible because it violates the law of conservation of energy. Instead, mechanical work done by an external agent against the opposing magnetic force is transformed into electrical energy, which is subsequently dissipated as Joule heat.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of energy.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q07 - Motional electromotive force in a moving conductor

questiontext.text: A straight conducting rod of length \( l \) moves with a constant speed \( v \) perpendicular to its own length and perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field \( B \). The motional electromotive force developed across the ends of the rod is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Conductor length is \( l \), speed of translation is \( v \), and the uniform magnetic field is \( B \). The vectors representing the rod length, velocity, and magnetic field are mutually orthogonal.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field is time-independent and uniform across the space swept by the rod. Resistance losses in moving the rod are ignored.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnetic flux enclosed by a sliding rectangular loop is \( \Phi_B = B l x \). By Faraday's law, \( \varepsilon = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} = -B l \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \). With \( \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = -v \), the induced emf is \( \varepsilon = B l v \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Alternatively, free charges \( q \) inside the rod experience a magnetic Lorentz force \( F = q v B \). The work done in moving a charge along the rod length \( l \) is \( W = q v B l \). The emf is work per unit charge: \( \varepsilon = \frac{W}{q} = B l v \).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking dimensions: \( [B][l][v] = [\text{M T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-1}][\text{L}][\text{L T}^{-1}] = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}] = [\text{V}] \). The motional electromotive force is \( B l v \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q08 - Dimensional formula of coefficient of self induction

questiontext.text: The dimensional formula of self-inductance \( L \) (as well as mutual inductance \( M \)) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Self-inductance \( L \) is defined through the flux linkage relation \( N \Phi_B = L I \), or the induced emf relation \( |\varepsilon| = L \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The number of turns \( N \) is dimensionless. Standard SI base dimensions are mass \( [\text{M}] \), length \( [\text{L}] \), time \( [\text{T}] \), and electric current \( [\text{A}] \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From \( L = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{\mathrm{d}I/\mathrm{d}t} \):
Electromotive force has dimensions of potential: \( [\varepsilon] = \frac{[\text{Work}]}{[\text{Charge}]} = \frac{[\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2}]}{[\text{A T}]} = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}] \).
Rate of change of current: \( [\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}] = [\text{A T}^{-1}] \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ [L] = \frac{[\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-3} \text{A}^{-1}]}{[\text{A T}^{-1}]} = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-2}] \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Energy stored in an inductor is \( U = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 \implies [L] = \frac{[U]}{[I^2]} = \frac{[\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2}]}{[\text{A}^2]} = [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-2}] \). The correct dimensional formula is \( [\text{M L}^2 \text{T}^{-2} \text{A}^{-2}] \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q09 - Mechanical analogue of self inductance in physics

questiontext.text: In electrical circuits, self-inductance \( L \) opposes any change (growth or decay) of electric current, playing the role of electrical inertia. This property is directly analogous to which mechanical quantity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In mechanics, inertia is the property of a body by virtue of which it opposes any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. Mass \( m \) is the quantitative measure of linear mechanical inertia.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
In an inductive circuit, the self-induced back emf \( \varepsilon = -L \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} \) opposes any increase or decrease in electric current \( I \), meaning work must be done against this back emf to establish a current.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
The magnetic energy stored in an inductor is \( U_B = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 \), which has the exact mathematical form of the kinetic energy of a particle \( K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \). Here, current \( I \) corresponds to velocity \( v \), and self-inductance \( L \) corresponds to mass \( m \).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Self-inductance is the electromagnetic analogue of mass in mechanics.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q10 - Condition for peak electromotive force in generator

questiontext.text: An alternating current (AC) generator armature coil rotates with constant angular speed in a uniform magnetic field. The instantaneous induced electromotive force reaches its maximum (peak) value when the angle \( \theta \) between the area vector \( \mathbf{A} \) of the coil and the magnetic field vector \( \mathbf{B} \) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The coil rotates with angular velocity \( \omega \) such that \( \theta = \omega t \). The magnetic flux linked with the coil is \( \Phi_B = B A \cos\theta = B A \cos\omega t \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field \( B \) is uniform, and the rotation axis is perpendicular to \( B \). At \( t = 0 \), the coil plane is perpendicular to the field (\( \theta = 0 \)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Faraday's law gives the instantaneous induced emf for an \( N \)-turn coil as:
\[ \varepsilon = -N \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} = -N B A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(\cos\omega t) = N B A \omega \sin\omega t \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The sine function \( \sin\theta = \sin\omega t \) attains its extremum values of \( \pm 1 \) when \( \theta = 90^\circ \) or \( \theta = 270^\circ \). At these orientations, the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field lines, and the rate of change of magnetic flux is greatest.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Peak electromotive force occurs when \( \theta = 90^\circ \) or \( 270^\circ \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q11 - Observation in primary secondary coil tapping experiment

questiontext.text: Two stationary coaxial coils, \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \), are placed side by side. Coil \( C_1 \) is connected to a sensitive galvanometer, while coil \( C_2 \) is connected to a DC battery through a tapping key. What is observed on the galvanometer when the tapping key is held pressed continuously?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Faraday's law dictates that an induced electromotive force and resultant electric current in a stationary closed coil depend strictly on the time rate of change of magnetic flux through the coil, \( \varepsilon = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \).

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
When the tapping key is pressed initially, current in coil \( C_2 \) grows from zero to its steady-state value, causing a changing magnetic flux in coil \( C_1 \) and producing a momentary deflection.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
Once the key is held pressed continuously, the current in coil \( C_2 \) becomes constant. The magnetic field produced by coil \( C_2 \) is steady, resulting in zero rate of change of magnetic flux through coil \( C_1 \) (\( \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \)). Therefore, no induced emf or current exists.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
No deflection is observed in the galvanometer while the key is held pressed continuously.

answer.text: A steady non-zero deflection is maintained continuously
The deflection increases linearly with elapsed time
No deflection is observed in the galvanometer
The pointer oscillates back and forth continuously with fixed amplitude

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q12 - Effect of iron core insertion in induction

questiontext.text: In Faraday's experiment with two stationary adjacent coils (primary coil with key and battery, secondary coil with galvanometer), what occurs when a soft iron rod is inserted along the common axis of the coils?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The magnetic flux linkage between two coils is given by \( N_1 \Phi_1 = M I_2 \), where the mutual inductance \( M \) depends directly on the magnetic permeability of the medium filling the space within the coils.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
Soft iron is a ferromagnetic material with a high relative magnetic permeability (\( \mu_r \gg 1 \)). Inserting an iron rod replaces the air core with a high-permeability medium, causing the magnetic flux density produced by a given current to increase by a factor of \( \mu_r \).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
When the key is tapped or released, the rate of change of magnetic flux \( \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_B}{\mathrm{d}t} \) linked with the secondary coil increases dramatically, generating a much larger induced emf and a dramatically larger galvanometer deflection.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The galvanometer deflection increases dramatically due to the increased magnetic permeability of the soft iron core.

answer.text: The deflection drops to zero because iron shields magnetic field lines
The deflection remains completely unchanged because current is unchanged
The deflection reverses direction while its magnitude decreases
The deflection increases dramatically due to increased magnetic permeability

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q13 - Calculation of magnetic flux through tilted plane

questiontext.text: A flat square coil of side \( 20\text{ cm} \) is placed in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude \( 0.50\text{ T} \). If the plane of the coil makes an angle of \( 30^\circ \) with the direction of the magnetic field lines, what is the magnetic flux linked with the coil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Side of the square coil: \( s = 20\text{ cm} = 0.20\text{ m} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.50\text{ T} \).
Angle between the plane of the coil and the magnetic field lines: \( \alpha = 30^\circ \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The area vector \( \mathbf{A} \) is perpendicular to the plane of the coil. Therefore, the angle \( \theta \) between the area vector \( \mathbf{A} \) and the magnetic field \( \mathbf{B} \) is \( \theta = 90^\circ - \alpha = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Area of the square coil: \( A = s^2 \).
Magnetic flux: \( \Phi_B = B A \cos\theta \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate area: \( A = (0.20\text{ m})^2 = 0.040\text{ m}^2 \).
Calculate flux:
\[ \Phi_B = (0.50\text{ T}) \times (0.040\text{ m}^2) \times \cos 60^\circ = 0.020 \times 0.5 = 0.010\text{ Wb} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ Wb} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units and magnitude: \( 0.50 \times 0.04 \times 0.5 = 0.01\text{ Wb} \). The magnetic flux linked with the coil is \( 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ Wb} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q14 - Induced electromotive force in vertical square loop

questiontext.text: A square loop of side \( 10\text{ cm} \) and electrical resistance \( 0.50\ \Omega \) is placed vertically in the east-west plane. A uniform magnetic field of \( 0.10\text{ T} \) is directed across the plane in the north-east direction. If the magnetic field is decreased to zero steadily in \( 0.70\text{ s} \), what are the magnitudes of the induced electromotive force and electric current during this time interval? (Take \( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Side of square loop: \( s = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m} \).
Loop resistance: \( R = 0.50\ \Omega \).
Initial magnetic field: \( B = 0.10\text{ T} \).
Final magnetic field: \( B_f = 0\text{ T} \).
Time interval: \( \Delta t = 0.70\text{ s} \).
Loop is in east-west plane, so normal vector points north (or south). The magnetic field is in the north-east direction, making an angle \( \theta = 45^\circ \) with the area vector.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The magnetic field decreases at a constant rate, so the induced emf is steady over the interval.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Area: \( A = s^2 = (0.10)^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ m}^2 \).
Initial flux: \( \Phi_i = B A \cos 45^\circ = \frac{0.10 \times 10^{-2}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{10^{-3}}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ Wb} \).
Final flux: \( \Phi_f = 0 \).
Induced emf magnitude: \( \varepsilon = \frac{|\Delta \Phi_B|}{\Delta t} \).
Induced current: \( I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{10^{-3}}{\sqrt{2} \times 0.70} = \frac{10^{-3}}{1.414 \times 0.70} = \frac{10^{-3}}{0.9898} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} = 1.0\text{ mV} \]
\[ I = \frac{\varepsilon}{R} = \frac{1.01 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V}}{0.50\ \Omega} \approx 2.02 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A} = 2.0\text{ mA} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking values: \( \varepsilon \approx 1.0\text{ mV} \) and \( I \approx 2.0\text{ mA} \). Both values match standard precision.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q15 - Electromotive force in rotated circular coil turns

questiontext.text: A circular coil of radius \( 10\text{ cm} \), consisting of \( 500 \) turns and electrical resistance \( 2.0\ \Omega \), is placed with its plane perpendicular to the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field (\( B_H = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \)). The coil is rotated through \( 180^\circ \) about its vertical diameter in \( 0.25\text{ s} \). What is the estimated magnitude of the average induced electromotive force in the coil? (Take \( \pi \approx 3.1416 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of coil: \( r = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m} \).
Number of turns: \( N = 500 \).
Resistance: \( R = 2.0\ \Omega \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 3.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T} \).
Rotation angle: \( 180^\circ \).
Time interval: \( \Delta t = 0.25\text{ s} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Initially, the area vector is aligned with the magnetic field (\( \theta_i = 0^\circ \)). After rotation through \( 180^\circ \), \( \theta_f = 180^\circ \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Area: \( A = \pi r^2 = \pi (0.10)^2 = 0.01 \pi\text{ m}^2 \).
Initial flux per turn: \( \Phi_i = B A \cos 0^\circ = B A \).
Final flux per turn: \( \Phi_f = B A \cos 180^\circ = -B A \).
Change in flux per turn: \( \Delta \Phi = \Phi_f - \Phi_i = -2 B A \).
Average induced emf magnitude: \( \varepsilon = N \frac{|\Delta \Phi|}{\Delta t} = \frac{2 N B A}{\Delta t} \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ B A = (3.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}) \times (0.01 \pi\text{ m}^2) = 3.0\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ Wb} \]
\[ 2 B A = 6.0\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ Wb} \approx 1.885 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Wb} \]
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{500 \times 6.0\pi \times 10^{-7}}{0.25} = 2000 \times 6.0\pi \times 10^{-7} = 1.2\pi \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \approx 3.77 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking: \( 1.2 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-3} = 3.77 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \). The estimated induced emf is \( 3.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q16 - Induced charge dependence on magnetic flux variation

questiontext.text: A closed conducting loop of total electrical resistance \( R \) is subjected to a changing magnetic flux. If the magnetic flux linked with the loop changes from an initial value \( \Phi_1 \) to a final value \( \Phi_2 \) over an arbitrary time interval \( \Delta t \), the total electric charge \( \Delta Q \) that flows through any cross-section of the wire is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The closed loop has fixed resistance \( R \). The flux changes by \( \Delta \Phi = \Phi_2 - \Phi_1 \) over duration \( \Delta t \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Self-inductance of the loop is assumed negligible so that current instantaneously satisfies Ohm's law.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Faraday's law, instantaneous induced emf is \( |\varepsilon| = \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \).
The instantaneous induced current is \( I = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t} \).
The net charge flown is \( \Delta Q = \int I \,\mathrm{d}t \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \Delta Q = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \frac{1}{R}\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\mathrm{d}t = \frac{1}{R} \int_{\Phi_1}^{\Phi_2} \mathrm{d}\Phi = \frac{|\Phi_2 - \Phi_1|}{R} \]
Notice that \( \Delta Q \) depends purely on the net change in flux and resistance, and is completely independent of the time interval \( \Delta t \) or the rate of flux change.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking dimensions: \( [\text{Wb}]/[\Omega] = [\text{V}\cdot\text{s}]/[\text{V/A}] = [\text{A}\cdot\text{s}] = [\text{C}] \). The total induced charge is \( \frac{|\Phi_2 - \Phi_1|}{R} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q17 - Induced current sense in entering rectangular loop

questiontext.text: A planar rectangular conducting loop is moved horizontally with constant velocity into a region containing a uniform magnetic field directed perpendicularly into the plane of the page. According to Lenz's law, while the loop is entering the field region:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lenz's law states that an induced electric current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
As the rectangular loop enters the field directed into the page, the area enclosed within the magnetic field increases, meaning the inward magnetic flux linked with the loop increases with time.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
To oppose this increase in inward flux, the induced current must produce an opposing magnetic field directed perpendicularly outwards (towards the reader). By the right-hand grip rule, an outward magnetic field requires an anticlockwise (counter-clockwise) circulation of current around the loop.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The induced current circulates in an anticlockwise direction to produce an outward magnetic field.

answer.text: The induced current circulates in an anticlockwise direction to produce an outward magnetic field
The induced current circulates in a clockwise direction to produce an inward magnetic field
No induced current flows because the velocity of the loop is constant
The induced current alternates symmetrically back and forth with high frequency

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q18 - Comparison of induced emf in leaving loops

questiontext.text: A rectangular loop and a circular loop are both pulled out of a region of uniform perpendicular magnetic field into a field-free region with a constant velocity \( v \). During their passage out of the field, the induced electromotive force:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
By Faraday's law of induction, the magnitude of the induced emf is \( \varepsilon = B \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} \), where \( \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} \) is the time rate at which the area of the loop inside the magnetic field region changes.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
For a rectangular loop moving perpendicular to its straight edge of constant length \( b \), the area inside the field decreases at a rate \( \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} = b \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = b v \). Because \( b \) and \( v \) are constants, \( \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} \) is constant, producing a constant induced emf \( \varepsilon = B b v \).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
For a circular loop, the length of the chord intersecting the boundary of the field region varies continuously as the loop exits. Therefore, the rate of change of area \( \frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}t} \) is not constant, causing the induced emf to vary with time throughout the exit.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The induced electromotive force is constant for the rectangular loop, but varies with time for the circular loop.

answer.text: Is constant for both the rectangular loop and the circular loop
Is constant for the rectangular loop, but varies with time for the circular loop
Is constant for the circular loop, but varies with time for the rectangular loop
Varies with time for both loops because their area inside the field decreases

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q19 - Polarities of capacitor plates between approaching magnets

questiontext.text: A circular wire loop contains an open gap connected to a parallel-plate capacitor with plates marked \( A \) (upper) and \( B \) (lower). A bar magnet with its South pole facing the loop approaches from the left, and another bar magnet with its North pole facing the loop approaches symmetrically from the right. What is the resulting polarity of plate \( A \) relative to plate \( B \)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Lenz's law, the induced current in a conducting loop must produce magnetic poles that oppose the motion of approaching magnetic poles.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
When the South pole approaches from the left side, the left face of the loop develops South polarity (clockwise current when viewed from the left). When the North pole approaches from the right side, the right face of the loop develops North polarity (anticlockwise current when viewed from the right). These two views are completely consistent and correspond to the exact same circulation of current in the loop.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
This induced circulation drives positive charge carriers in the wire towards plate \( A \) and pulls positive charges away from plate \( B \) (or deposits electrons onto plate \( B \)). Consequently, plate \( A \) accumulates positive charge while plate \( B \) accumulates negative charge.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Plate \( A \) becomes positive with respect to plate \( B \).

answer.text: Plate \( A \) becomes negative with respect to plate \( B \)
Both plates remain uncharged because the two approaching magnets cancel out
Plate \( A \) becomes positive with respect to plate \( B \)
The plates acquire alternating polarities oscillating at high frequency

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q20 - Direction of induced current in expanding loop

questiontext.text: A closed flexible conducting loop of irregular shape lies in the plane of the page inside an external uniform magnetic field directed perpendicularly into the page. When the loop is deformed into a circular shape, what is the direction of the induced current in the loop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a given fixed perimeter, a circle encloses the maximum possible geometric area. Therefore, when an irregular loop is transformed into a circle, its enclosed surface area increases.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
Because the external magnetic field is directed perpendicularly into the page, an increase in the enclosed area causes the inward magnetic flux linked with the loop to increase with time.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
According to Lenz's law, the induced current must flow in a direction that opposes the increase in inward magnetic flux. Thus, it must produce an opposing magnetic field pointing perpendicularly out of the page. By the right-hand rule, an outward magnetic field is generated by an anticlockwise current circulation around the loop.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The induced current flows in an anticlockwise direction to oppose the increase in magnetic flux.

answer.text: Clockwise, to assist the increase in magnetic flux
Zero, because the external magnetic field is constant in time
Anticlockwise, to oppose the increase in magnetic flux

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q21 - Electromotive force in rotating metallic rod spoke

questiontext.text: A straight metallic rod of length \( 1.0\text{ m} \) is rotated with an angular frequency of \( 400\text{ rad s}^{-1} \) about an axis normal to the rod passing through one of its ends. The other end of the rod is in continuous sliding contact with a circular metallic ring. A constant and uniform magnetic field of \( 0.50\text{ T} \) parallel to the rotation axis exists everywhere. What is the electromotive force developed between the central axis and the metallic ring?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of rotating rod: \( R = 1.0\text{ m} \).
Angular frequency: \( \omega = 400\text{ rad s}^{-1} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.50\text{ T} \).
Axis of rotation is parallel to the magnetic field.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The rod is rotated in a plane perpendicular to the uniform magnetic field. Frictional resistance and contact potential are negligible.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
An element of the rod of length \( \mathrm{d}r \) at distance \( r \) from the centre moves with linear speed \( v = \omega r \).
The motional emf across the element is \( \mathrm{d}\varepsilon = B v \,\mathrm{d}r = B \omega r \,\mathrm{d}r \).
Integrating from \( r = 0 \) to \( r = R \):
\[ \varepsilon = \int_0^R B \omega r \,\mathrm{d}r = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.50\text{ T}) \times (400\text{ rad s}^{-1}) \times (1.0\text{ m})^2 \]
\[ \varepsilon = 0.25 \times 400 = 100\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking units: \( \text{T} \cdot \text{s}^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^2 = \text{Wb/s} = \text{V} \). The induced electromotive force developed is \( 100\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q22 - Induced electromotive force in rotating wheel spokes

questiontext.text: A wheel with \( 10 \) metallic spokes, each of length \( 0.50\text{ m} \), is rotated with a speed of \( 120\text{ rev/min} \) in a plane normal to the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field (\( B_H = 0.40\text{ G} = 0.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \)). What is the induced electromotive force between the central axle and the rim of the wheel? (Take \( \pi \approx 3.1416 \))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of spokes: \( N = 10 \).
Length of each spoke: \( R = 0.50\text{ m} \).
Rotational speed: \( \nu = 120\text{ rev/min} = \frac{120}{60}\text{ rev/s} = 2.0\text{ rev/s} \).
Magnetic field: \( B = 0.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All \( 10 \) spokes are identical and connected in parallel between the common axle and the outer conducting rim. Therefore, the total emf between the axle and the rim is equal to the emf generated across a single spoke.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Angular velocity: \( \omega = 2\pi \nu = 2\pi \times 2.0 = 4\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1} \).
Induced emf across a rotating spoke: \( \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} B \omega R^2 \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.40 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}) \times (4\pi\text{ rad s}^{-1}) \times (0.50\text{ m})^2 \]
\[ \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \times (0.40 \times 10^{-4}) \times (4\pi) \times 0.25 \]
\[ \varepsilon = 0.40 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 0.20\pi \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.20 \times 3.1416 \times 10^{-4} = 6.2832 \times 10^{-5}\text{ V} \approx 6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The number of spokes is immaterial because they are connected in parallel. The induced emf is \( 6.28 \times 10^{-5}\text{ V} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q23 - Potential difference in falling horizontal copper wire

questiontext.text: A horizontal straight conducting wire of length \( 10\text{ m} \) extending from east to west falls vertically with a speed of \( 5.0\text{ m s}^{-1} \) perpendicular to the horizontal component of the Earth's magnetic field, \( 0.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ Wb m}^{-2} \) (directed horizontally northward). What is the instantaneous induced emf and which end of the wire is at higher electrical potential?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of wire: \( l = 10\text{ m} \) (oriented along east-west).
Falling velocity: \( \mathbf{v} = 5.0\text{ m s}^{-1} \) (directed vertically downwards).
Horizontal magnetic field: \( \mathbf{B} = 0.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T} \) (directed northward).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Directions: North = \( +\hat{j} \), East = \( +\hat{i} \), Downward = \( -\hat{k} \).
The magnetic Lorentz force on a positive test charge \( q \) is \( \mathbf{F} = q (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Magnitude of motional emf: \( \varepsilon = B l v \).
Direction of force on positive charges: \( \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \).
With \( \mathbf{v} \) downwards and \( \mathbf{B} \) northward, the cross product points towards the West: \( (-\hat{k}) \times (+\hat{j}) = +\hat{i} \) (or using the right-hand rule, fingers from down to north curl towards west).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \varepsilon = (0.30 \times 10^{-4}\text{ T}) \times (10\text{ m}) \times (5.0\text{ m s}^{-1}) = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ V} = 1.5\text{ mV} \]
Because positive charges are pushed towards the western end (and free electrons are driven towards the eastern end), positive charge accumulates at the western end. Therefore, the western end is at higher electrical potential.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude is \( 1.5\text{ mV} \) and the western end is at higher electrical potential.

answer.text: \( 1.5\text{ mV} \), and the eastern end is at higher potential
\( 3.0\text{ mV} \), and the western end is at higher potential
\( 1.5\text{ mV} \), and the western end is at higher potential
\( 3.0\text{ mV} \), and the eastern end is at higher potential

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q24 - Microscopic origin of motional electromotive force derivation

questiontext.text: When a straight conducting rod of length \( l \) moves with constant velocity \( \mathbf{v} \) across a perpendicular magnetic field \( \mathbf{B} \), mobile charge carriers experience a magnetic Lorentz force. The induced motional electromotive force \( \varepsilon = B l v \) fundamentally represents:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electromotive force (emf) is defined as the work done by a non-electrostatic force per unit electric charge in moving the charge between two terminals or around a complete circuit.

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
In a moving rod, every mobile charge carrier of charge \( q \) moves through magnetic field \( \mathbf{B} \) with velocity \( \mathbf{v} \), experiencing a magnetic Lorentz force of magnitude \( F_m = q v B \) directed along the length of the rod.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
The work done by this magnetic force in displacing a charge carrier through the full conductor length \( l \) is \( W = F_m l = q v B l \). Dividing this work by the charge \( q \) gives the electromotive force: \( \varepsilon = \frac{W}{q} = B l v \).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The motional electromotive force fundamentally represents the work done per unit electric charge by the magnetic Lorentz force in moving carriers across the rod.

answer.text: The electrostatic potential energy created by fixed positive atomic lattice cores
The thermal dissipation energy per unit time within the conductor crystal structure
The rate of change of the intrinsic electrostatic capacitance of the moving rod
The work done per unit electric charge by the magnetic Lorentz force in moving carriers across the rod

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q25 - Scaling of mutual inductance of coaxial solenoids

questiontext.text: Two long coaxial solenoids of the same length \( l \) have radii \( r_1 \) and \( r_2 \) (with \( r_1 < r_2 \)) and turn densities \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \) turns per unit length, respectively. If the number of turns per unit length of both solenoids is doubled while keeping their lengths and radii unchanged, the mutual inductance of the pair will:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial turn densities are \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \). Solenoid length is \( l \), and inner radius is \( r_1 \). The new turn densities are \( n_1' = 2 n_1 \) and \( n_2' = 2 n_2 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The solenoids are long (\( l \gg r_2 \)), so end effects can be neglected. The core medium is air.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids is given by:
\[ M = \mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the new turn densities:
\[ M' = \mu_0 (2 n_1) (2 n_2) \pi r_1^2 l = 4 (\mu_0 n_1 n_2 \pi r_1^2 l) = 4 M \]
Because mutual inductance is directly proportional to the product \( n_1 n_2 \), doubling both values multiplies the mutual inductance by a factor of \( 2 \times 2 = 4 \).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The mutual inductance increases by a factor of 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q26 - Reciprocity relation between mutual inductance coefficients

questiontext.text: For two arbitrary stationary coils, Coil 1 and Coil 2, placed in fixed relative orientations in a non-magnetic medium, the coefficient of mutual induction of Coil 1 with respect to Coil 2 (\( M_{12} \)) and that of Coil 2 with respect to Coil 1 (\( M_{21} \)) satisfy:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mutual inductance measures the magnetic flux linked with one circuit due to unit electric current flowing in another adjacent circuit: \( N_1 \Phi_1 = M_{12} I_2 \) and \( N_2 \Phi_2 = M_{21} I_1 \).

Step 2: Analysis and Evaluation
Even when the two coils possess completely different geometries, cross-sectional areas, or numbers of turns (such that calculating the non-uniform magnetic flux in one direction is mathematically difficult), the reciprocity theorem of electromagnetism applies.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Deduction
By electromagnetic reciprocity, the mutual inductance is symmetric: \( M_{12} = M_{21} = M \). The coupling coefficient between two circuits in a linear medium is strictly independent of which coil is treated as primary and which as secondary.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\( M_{12} = M_{21} \), regardless of whether the coils have different shapes, radii, or number of turns.

answer.text: \( M_{12} > M_{21} \) whenever coil 1 has a larger cross-sectional area than coil 2
\( M_{12} = M_{21} \), regardless of whether the coils have different shapes, radii, or number of turns
\( M_{12} / M_{21} = N_1 / N_2 \), proportional to the ratio of their total turns
\( M_{12} / M_{21} = (N_1 / N_2)^2 \), proportional to the square of their turns ratio

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q27 - Mutual inductance between concentric unequal circular loops

questiontext.text: Two flat circular coils of single turn are placed coplanar with concentric centres. The inner coil has a small radius \( r_1 \) and the outer coil has a much larger radius \( r_2 \) (such that \( r_1 \ll r_2 \)). What is the mutual inductance \( M \) of this arrangement in vacuum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Inner circular coil radius: \( r_1 \).
Outer circular coil radius: \( r_2 \), with \( r_1 \ll r_2 \).
Both coils are coplanar and concentric.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because \( r_1 \ll r_2 \), the magnetic field produced by current \( I_2 \) in the outer coil can be treated as uniform across the small area of the inner coil.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Magnetic field at the centre of the outer circular coil carrying current \( I_2 \):
\[ B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2 r_2} \]
Flux linked with the inner coil: \( \Phi_1 = B_2 A_1 = B_2 (\pi r_1^2) \).
Mutual inductance definition: \( \Phi_1 = M_{12} I_2 \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ \Phi_1 = \left(\frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2 r_2}\right) (\pi r_1^2) = \left(\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2 r_2}\right) I_2 \]
Therefore:
\[ M = M_{12} = M_{21} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2 r_2} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensions: \( [\mu_0][\text{length}] = [\text{H/m}][\text{m}] = [\text{H}] \). The mutual inductance is \( \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_1^2}{2 r_2} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q28 - Magnetic flux linkage change in coupled coils

questiontext.text: A pair of adjacent coils has a mutual inductance of \( 1.5\text{ H} \). If the electric current in one coil changes from \( 0 \) to \( 20\text{ A} \) in \( 0.50\text{ s} \), what is the total change of magnetic flux linkage with the other coil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mutual inductance: \( M = 1.5\text{ H} \).
Initial current: \( I_1 = 0\text{ A} \).
Final current: \( I_2 = 20\text{ A} \).
Time interval: \( \Delta t = 0.50\text{ s} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The flux linkage in the secondary coil is directly proportional to the current in the primary coil: \( N_2 \Phi_2 = M I_1 \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Change of magnetic flux linkage:
\[ \Delta(N_2 \Phi_2) = M \,\Delta I \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Change in current: \( \Delta I = 20\text{ A} - 0\text{ A} = 20\text{ A} \).
\[ \Delta(N_2 \Phi_2) = (1.5\text{ H}) \times (20\text{ A}) = 30\text{ Wb} \]
Note that the duration of \( 0.50\text{ s} \) is relevant only if calculating average emf, but the total change in flux linkage depends solely on \( M \) and \( \Delta I \).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\( 1.5\text{ H} \times 20\text{ A} = 30\text{ Wb} \). The total change of magnetic flux linkage is \( 30\text{ Wb} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q29 - Self inductance of solenoid with magnetic core

questiontext.text: A long air-core solenoid has a self-inductance of \( L_0 = 2.0\text{ mH} \). If the core of the solenoid is completely filled with a ferromagnetic material of relative permeability \( \mu_r = 800 \), what is the new self-inductance of the solenoid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial self-inductance with air core: \( L_0 = 2.0\text{ mH} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H} \).
Relative permeability of core material: \( \mu_r = 800 \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The solenoid geometry (length \( l \), cross-sectional area \( A \), and number of turns \( N \)) remains unchanged, and the material completely fills the volume containing magnetic field lines.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Air-core self-inductance: \( L_0 = \mu_0 n^2 A l \).
Self-inductance with magnetic core: \( L = \mu_r \mu_0 n^2 A l = \mu_r L_0 \).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ L = 800 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}) = 1.6\text{ H} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying: \( 800 \times 2\text{ mH} = 1600\text{ mH} = 1.6\text{ H} \). The new self-inductance is \( 1.6\text{ H} \).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_INDUCTION_MCQ_Q30 - Estimation of self inductance from falling current

questiontext.text: The electric current in an inductive circuit falls steadily from \( 5.0\text{ A} \) to \( 0.0\text{ A} \) in \( 0.10\text{ s} \). If an average electromotive force of \( 200\text{ V} \) is induced in the circuit, what is the estimated self-inductance of the circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial current: \( I_1 = 5.0\text{ A} \).
Final current: \( I_2 = 0.0\text{ A} \).
Time interval: \( \Delta t = 0.10\text{ s} \).
Induced emf magnitude: \( |\varepsilon| = 200\text{ V} \).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The current decreases at a uniform steady rate, so \( \frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The self-induced electromotive force is given by:
\[ |\varepsilon| = L \left|\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}\right| \implies L = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{|\Delta I| / \Delta t} \]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
