Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Current is expressed as \(i = i_m \sin(\omega t + \phi)\) relative to voltage \(v = v_m \sin\omega t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The phase angle is given by \(\tan\phi = \frac{X_C - X_L}{R}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the tangent of the phase angle:
\[ \tan\phi = \frac{4\ \Omega - 8\ \Omega}{3\ \Omega} = -\frac{4}{3} \approx -1.333 \]
Find the angle:
\[ \phi = \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx -53.13^\circ \approx -53.1^\circ \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \(X_L > X_C\), the circuit is inductive, and current lags voltage, indicated by negative \(\phi = -53.1^\circ\).

Final Answer: \(-53.1^\circ\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q25 - Angular frequency of free LC tank oscillations

questiontext.text: A fully charged \(30\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is connected to a \(27\text{ mH}\) inductor. What is the angular frequency of free oscillations of this circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance \(C = 30\ \mu\text{F} = 30 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), inductance \(L = 27\text{ mH} = 27 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Resistance of the loop is zero, corresponding to undamped harmonic oscillations.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The natural angular frequency of an LC oscillator is \(\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the product \(LC\):
\[ LC = (27 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}) \times (30 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}) = 810 \times 10^{-9}\text{ s}^2 = 81 \times 10^{-8}\text{ s}^2 \]
Take the square root:
\[ \sqrt{LC} = \sqrt{81 \times 10^{-8}} = 9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s} \]
Calculate \(\omega\):
\[ \omega = \frac{1}{9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}} = \frac{10000}{9}\text{ rad/s} \approx 1111.1\text{ rad/s} \approx 1.11 \times 10^3\text{ rad/s} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dimensions: \([1/\sqrt{LC}] = \text{s}^{-1} = \text{rad/s}\). Value is \(1.11 \times 10^3\text{ rad/s}\).

Final Answer: \(1.11 \times 10^3\text{ rad/s}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q26 - Resonant frequency of circuit with given parameters

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit has \(L = 25.48\text{ mH}\) and \(C = 796\ \mu\text{F}\). What is the resonant angular frequency \(\omega_0\) and the corresponding linear frequency \(\nu_r\) of this circuit? (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Inductance \(L = 25.48\text{ mH} = 25.48 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}\), capacitance \(C = 796\ \mu\text{F} = 796 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Resonance occurs when inductive reactance equals capacitive reactance.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resonant angular frequency is \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), and linear resonant frequency is \(\nu_r = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the product \(LC\):
\[ LC = (25.48 \times 10^{-3}) \times (796 \times 10^{-6}) = 2.0282 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}^2 \]
Compute \(\sqrt{LC}\):
\[ \sqrt{LC} = \sqrt{2.0282 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 4.5036 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s} \]
Compute \(\omega_0\):
\[ \omega_0 = \frac{1}{4.5036 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}} \approx 222.05\text{ rad/s} \approx 222.1\text{ rad/s} \]
Compute \(\nu_r\):
\[ \nu_r = \frac{222.05}{2 \times 3.14}\text{ Hz} = \frac{222.05}{6.28}\text{ Hz} \approx 35.36\text{ Hz} \approx 35.4\text{ Hz} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Values conform to Example 7.9 of the textbook: \(\omega_0 = 222.1\text{ rad/s}\) and \(\nu_r = 35.4\text{ Hz}\).

Final Answer: \(\omega_0 = 222.1\text{ rad/s}\) and \(\nu_r = 35.4\text{ Hz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q27 - Power dissipated and current at resonant condition

questiontext.text: A sinusoidal voltage of peak value \(283\text{ V}\) is applied to a series LCR circuit with resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\). If the source frequency is tuned to the resonant frequency, what are the root-mean-square current and the power dissipated at resonance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Peak voltage \(v_m = 283\text{ V}\), resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\), circuit tuned to resonance.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At resonance, total impedance is purely resistive (\(Z = R\)) and power factor is \(\cos\phi = 1\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Root-mean-square voltage is \(V = \frac{v_m}{\sqrt{2}}\). Current at resonance is \(I = \frac{V}{R}\). Power dissipated is \(P = I^2 R\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate root-mean-square voltage:
\[ V = \frac{283\text{ V}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx \frac{283}{1.4142}\text{ V} \approx 200.11\text{ V} \approx 200\text{ V} \]
Calculate root-mean-square current:
\[ I = \frac{200.11\text{ V}}{3\ \Omega} \approx 66.70\text{ A} \approx 66.7\text{ A} \]
Calculate power dissipated:
\[ P = I^2 R = (66.70\text{ A})^2 \times 3\ \Omega = 4448.9 \times 3\text{ W} = 13346.7\text{ W} \approx 13.35\text{ kW} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check using \(P = \frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{(200.11)^2}{3} = \frac{40044}{3} \approx 13348\text{ W} = 13.35\text{ kW}\).

Final Answer: \(I = 66.7\text{ A}\) and \(P = 13.35\text{ kW}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q28 - Resonant frequency for five henry eighty microfarad

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit has \(L = 5.0\text{ H}\), \(C = 80\ \mu\text{F}\), and \(R = 40\ \Omega\) connected to a variable-frequency \(230\text{ V}\) source. What is the source frequency that drives the circuit into resonance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Inductance \(L = 5.0\text{ H}\), capacitance \(C = 80\ \mu\text{F} = 80 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), resistance \(R = 40\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The driving frequency equals the natural resonance frequency where net reactance cancels.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Resonant angular frequency is \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\), and linear frequency is \(\nu_0 = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(LC\):
\[ LC = 5.0 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}^2 = 400 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}^2 \]
Compute \(\omega_0\):
\[ \omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \times 10^{-4}}} = \frac{1}{2 \times 10^{-2}}\text{ rad/s} = 50\text{ rad/s} \]
Compute linear frequency \(\nu_0\):
\[ \nu_0 = \frac{50}{2 \times 3.1416}\text{ Hz} \approx \frac{50}{6.2832}\text{ Hz} \approx 7.958\text{ Hz} \approx 7.96\text{ Hz} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Values match NCERT Exercise 7.8(a): \(\omega_0 = 50\text{ rad/s}\) and \(\nu_0 = 7.96\text{ Hz}\).

Final Answer: \(\omega_0 = 50\text{ rad/s}\) and \(\nu_0 = 7.96\text{ Hz}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q29 - Current amplitude at resonant frequency in circuit

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit has \(L = 5.0\text{ H}\), \(C = 80\ \mu\text{F}\), and \(R = 40\ \Omega\) connected to a variable-frequency \(230\text{ V}\) source. What is the amplitude of the current \(i_m\) at the resonating frequency?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Supply root-mean-square voltage \(V = 230\text{ V}\), resistance \(R = 40\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At the resonating frequency, inductive reactance and capacitive reactance cancel, so impedance is \(Z = R\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Peak voltage amplitude is \(v_m = \sqrt{2} V\). Current amplitude is \(i_m = \frac{v_m}{R}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate peak voltage:
\[ v_m = \sqrt{2} \times 230\text{ V} \approx 1.4142 \times 230\text{ V} \approx 325.27\text{ V} \]
Calculate current amplitude:
\[ i_m = \frac{v_m}{R} = \frac{325.27\text{ V}}{40\ \Omega} \approx 8.1317\text{ A} \approx 8.13\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Root-mean-square current is \(I = \frac{230}{40} = 5.75\text{ A}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives \(5.75 \times 1.4142 = 8.13\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(8.13\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q30 - Reactive potential drops across inductor and capacitor

questiontext.text: In a series LCR circuit with \(L = 5.0\text{ H}\), \(C = 80\ \mu\text{F}\), and \(R = 40\ \Omega\) driven at resonance (\(\omega_0 = 50\text{ rad/s}\)) by a \(230\text{ V}\) supply, what are the root-mean-square voltages across the inductor and capacitor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(L = 5.0\text{ H}\), \(C = 80\ \mu\text{F}\), \(R = 40\ \Omega\), supply root-mean-square voltage \(V = 230\text{ V}\), \(\omega_0 = 50\text{ rad/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Circuit is at resonance; current is \(I = \frac{V}{R}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(X_L = \omega_0 L\), \(X_C = \frac{1}{\omega_0 C}\), \(V_L = I X_L\), \(V_C = I X_C\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate root-mean-square current:
\[ I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{230\text{ V}}{40\ \Omega} = 5.75\text{ A} \]
Calculate inductive reactance:
\[ X_L = \omega_0 L = 50\text{ rad/s} \times 5.0\text{ H} = 250\ \Omega \]
Calculate capacitive reactance:
\[ X_C = \frac{1}{50 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}}\ \Omega = \frac{1}{0.004}\ \Omega = 250\ \Omega \]
Calculate voltage drops:
\[ V_L = I X_L = 5.75\text{ A} \times 250\ \Omega = 1437.5\text{ V} \]
\[ V_C = I X_C = 5.75\text{ A} \times 250\ \Omega = 1437.5\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Because \(V_L\) and \(V_C\) are \(180^\circ\) out of phase, their phasor sum is \(V_L - V_C = 0\text{ V}\), even though each component carries \(1437.5\text{ V}\).

Final Answer: \(V_L = 1437.5\text{ V}\) and \(V_C = 1437.5\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q31 - Average power transferred to circuit at resonance

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit with \(R = 20\ \Omega\), \(L = 1.5\text{ H}\), and \(C = 35\ \mu\text{F}\) is connected to a variable-frequency \(200\text{ V}\) ac supply. When the supply frequency equals the natural resonant frequency of the circuit, what is the average power transferred per complete cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resistance \(R = 20\ \Omega\), inductance \(L = 1.5\text{ H}\), capacitance \(C = 35\ \mu\text{F}\), supply voltage \(V = 200\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The circuit operates at resonance, where impedance is minimum and equal to \(R\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
At resonance, power factor is \(\cos\phi = 1\), and average power is \(P = \frac{V^2}{R}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate root-mean-square current at resonance:
\[ I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{200\text{ V}}{20\ \Omega} = 10\text{ A} \]
Calculate average power:
\[ P = I^2 R = (10\text{ A})^2 \times 20\ \Omega = 100 \times 20\text{ W} = 2000\text{ W} = 2.0\text{ kW} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check: \(P = \frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{200^2}{20} = \frac{40000}{20} = 2000\text{ W} = 2.0\text{ kW}\). Matches NCERT Exercise 7.7.

Final Answer: \(2.0\text{ kW}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q32 - Power dissipated and power factor in series

questiontext.text: A sinusoidal voltage of peak value \(v_m = 283\text{ V}\) is applied to a series LCR circuit with resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\) and total impedance \(Z = 5\ \Omega\). What are the power factor of the circuit and the average power dissipated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Peak voltage \(v_m = 283\text{ V}\), resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\), impedance \(Z = 5\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Power dissipation takes place exclusively across the resistive element.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Power factor is \(\cos\phi = \frac{R}{Z}\). Current is \(I = \frac{v_m}{\sqrt{2} Z}\). Power dissipated is \(P = I^2 R\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the power factor:
\[ \cos\phi = \frac{3\ \Omega}{5\ \Omega} = 0.60 \]
Calculate peak current amplitude:
\[ i_m = \frac{v_m}{Z} = \frac{283\text{ V}}{5\ \Omega} = 56.6\text{ A} \]
Calculate root-mean-square current:
\[ I = \frac{i_m}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{56.6\text{ A}}{1.4142} \approx 40.02\text{ A} \approx 40\text{ A} \]
Calculate average power dissipated:
\[ P = I^2 R = (40\text{ A})^2 \times 3\ \Omega = 1600 \times 3\text{ W} = 4800\text{ W} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check using \(P = V I \cos\phi = \left(\frac{283}{\sqrt{2}}\right)(40)(0.6) = 200.1 \times 24 \approx 4802\text{ W} \approx 4800\text{ W}\).

Final Answer: \(\cos\phi = 0.60\) and \(P = 4800\text{ W}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q33 - Quality factor calculation for series resonant circuit

questiontext.text: A series resonant circuit has an inductor \(L = 1.0\text{ H}\), a capacitor \(C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}\), and a resistor \(R = 10\ \Omega\). What is the Quality factor \(Q\) of this circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Inductance \(L = 1.0\text{ H}\), capacitance \(C = 1.0\ \mu\text{F} = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), resistance \(R = 10\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The circuit is in resonance at its natural angular frequency \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Quality factor is defined as \(Q = \frac{\omega_0 L}{R} = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the ratio \(\frac{L}{C}\):
\[ \frac{L}{C} = \frac{1.0\text{ H}}{1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}} = 10^6\ \Omega^2 \]
Take the square root:
\[ \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \sqrt{10^6} = 10^3\ \Omega = 1000\ \Omega \]
Calculate the Quality factor:
\[ Q = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}} = \frac{1000\ \Omega}{10\ \Omega} = 100 \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(Q\) is a dimensionless quantity. \(\omega_0 = 1000\text{ rad/s}\), \(X_L = 1000\ \Omega\), and \(Q = X_L / R = 1000 / 10 = 100\).

Final Answer: \(100\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q34 - Resultant source voltage from branch potential drops

questiontext.text: In a series LCR circuit, the root-mean-square voltages measured across the resistor, inductor, and capacitor are \(V_R = 80\text{ V}\), \(V_L = 100\text{ V}\), and \(V_C = 40\text{ V}\) respectively. What is the root-mean-square voltage of the source?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(V_R = 80\text{ V}\), \(V_L = 100\text{ V}\), \(V_C = 40\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The individual component voltages are sinusoidal phasors with relative phase angles: \(V_R\) in phase with current, \(V_L\) leading by \(90^\circ\), \(V_C\) lagging by \(90^\circ\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total source voltage is given by the phasor resultant \(V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the net reactive voltage:
\[ V_L - V_C = 100\text{ V} - 40\text{ V} = 60\text{ V} \]
Combine with the resistive voltage using the Pythagorean theorem:
\[ V = \sqrt{(80\text{ V})^2 + (60\text{ V})^2} = \sqrt{6400 + 3600}\text{ V} = \sqrt{10000}\text{ V} = 100\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Simple algebraic addition gives \(80 + 100 + 40 = 220\text{ V}\), but phasor addition correctly accounts for phase differences to give \(100\text{ V}\).

Final Answer: \(100\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q35 - Ideal step-up transformer output voltage current

questiontext.text: An ideal step-up transformer has \(100\text{ turns}\) in the primary coil and \(200\text{ turns}\) in the secondary coil. When the primary is connected to a \(220\text{ V}\) supply drawing a current of \(10.0\text{ A}\), what are the secondary voltage and secondary current?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Primary turns \(N_p = 100\), secondary turns \(N_s = 200\), primary voltage \(V_p = 220\text{ V}\), primary current \(I_p = 10.0\text{ A}\). Ideal transformer (100% efficiency).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Zero flux leakage and negligible winding resistances.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Turns ratio relations: \(\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p}\), and power conservation \(V_p I_p = V_s I_s \implies \frac{I_s}{I_p} = \frac{N_p}{N_s}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate secondary voltage:
\[ V_s = \left(\frac{N_s}{N_p}\right) V_p = \left(\frac{200}{100}\right) \times 220\text{ V} = 2 \times 220\text{ V} = 440\text{ V} \]
Calculate secondary current:
\[ I_s = \left(\frac{N_p}{N_s}\right) I_p = \left(\frac{100}{200}\right) \times 10.0\text{ A} = 0.5 \times 10.0\text{ A} = 5.0\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Check input vs output power: \(P_{\text{in}} = 220 \times 10 = 2200\text{ W}\); \(P_{\text{out}} = 440 \times 5 = 2200\text{ W}\). Energy is conserved. \(V_s = 440\text{ V}\) and \(I_s = 5.0\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(V_s = 440\text{ V}\) and \(I_s = 5.0\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q36 - Efficiency and secondary current of real transformer

questiontext.text: A step-down transformer connected to a \(2200\text{ V}\) line supplies power at \(220\text{ V}\). The primary coil draws a current of \(5.0\text{ A}\). If the output power delivered by the secondary is \(9.9\text{ kW}\), what are the efficiency of the transformer and the secondary current?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Primary voltage \(V_p = 2200\text{ V}\), primary current \(I_p = 5.0\text{ A}\), secondary voltage \(V_s = 220\text{ V}\), output power \(P_s = 9.9\text{ kW} = 9900\text{ W}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Load is resistive with unity power factor.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Input power is \(P_p = V_p I_p\). Efficiency is \(\eta = \frac{P_s}{P_p} \times 100\%\). Secondary current is \(I_s = \frac{P_s}{V_s}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate input power:
\[ P_p = 2200\text{ V} \times 5.0\text{ A} = 11000\text{ W} = 11\text{ kW} \]
Calculate efficiency:
\[ \eta = \frac{9900\text{ W}}{11000\text{ W}} \times 100\% = 0.90 \times 100\% = 90\% \]
Calculate secondary current:
\[ I_s = \frac{9900\text{ W}}{220\text{ V}} = 45\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Output power \(9900\text{ W}\) divided by input power \(11000\text{ W}\) gives \(90\%\) efficiency. Secondary current is \(45\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(\text{Efficiency} = 90\%\) and \(I_s = 45\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ALTERNATING_CURRENT_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Operational stages of doorway metal detector

questiontext.text:
The following events describe the physical and operational stages of a walk-through airport security metal detector based on resonance in an AC circuit:

  1. The change in circuit current is detected by electronic circuitry, triggering an acoustic alarm.
  2. A person carrying a metallic item walks through the doorway coil.
  3. The circuit operates at resonance with a capacitor tuned to the coil's baseline inductance.
  4. The presence of metal changes the inductance of the coil, altering the circuit's impedance and significantly changing the current.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An airport metal detector functions on the principle of electrical resonance in an AC tuning circuit containing an inductor coil and a tuning capacitor. In the unperturbed state, the circuit is pre-tuned so that its natural resonant frequency matches the driving AC frequency, sustaining a steady resonant current.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Initial State
Initially, before any passenger enters, the doorway coil is connected to a tuning capacitor and is adjusted so that the circuit is in resonance. This provides the stable baseline reference condition.

Step 3: Progression of Operational Events
1. Baseline resonance: The coil is tuned to resonance with the capacitor.
2. Perturbation: A passenger carrying a metallic object enters and walks through the coil doorway.
3. Physical response: The metal object alters the magnetic permeability in the vicinity of the coil, thereby modifying the self-inductance of the coil. This alters the overall impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}\) of the circuit and causes a sharp shift away from the resonant condition, resulting in a significant change in the circuit current.
4. Detection and alert: The electronic monitoring circuitry detects this sudden change in current amplitude and triggers an audible alarm.

Step 4: Final Sequence
The correct logical and chronological order of stages is: circuit initially operating at baseline resonance, followed by the person walking through the coil with metal, followed by the modification of coil inductance and impedance causing a current shift, and finally the electronic detection triggering the alarm (III → II → IV → I).

Final Conceptual Answer: III → II → IV → I

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ALTERNATING_CURRENT_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequence of electrical power distribution grid

questiontext.text:
The following stages represent the sequence of events in the large-scale transmission and distribution of alternating current power from an electric generating plant to a household:

  1. Voltage is stepped down at local distributing substations and utility poles to reach 240 V.
  2. Electricity is generated at the power plant and its voltage is stepped up by a transformer to reduce line current and minimize \(I^2 R\) transmission heating loss.
  3. High-voltage electric power is transmitted over long distances through transmission lines to an area substation near consumers.
  4. Voltage is initially stepped down at an area substation for safe intermediate regional distribution.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order from power generation to domestic supply?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electric power transmission relies on transformers to maximize economic and energetic efficiency. Since Joule heat loss in transmission lines scales as \(I^2 R\), electric power is transmitted at extremely high voltages and low currents over long distances, then systematically stepped down in stages as it approaches consumers.

Step 2: Analysis of the Distribution Chain
1. Generation and Step-up: At the power station, mechanical or thermal energy is converted into electrical energy by generators. A step-up transformer increases the voltage significantly, reducing the transmission current by the inverse ratio (\(I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s\)), which cuts down the \(I^2 R\) dissipation in conductors.
2. Long-Distance Transmission: The stepped-up, low-current electricity is transmitted economically over long-distance grid conductors to the vicinity of consumer population centers.
3. Regional Substation Step-down: At an area substation near the consumer region, a step-down transformer lowers the high transmission voltage to intermediate distribution levels.
4. Local Distribution and Household Delivery: The voltage is progressively stepped down further at local distribution substations and utility-pole transformers before the safe, standard operating potential of 240 V enters homes and offices.

Step 3: Final Sequence
The correct sequence begins with voltage step-up at the generation plant, followed by long-distance transmission, followed by initial step-down at the area substation, and concluding with local step-down to 240 V for household outlets (II → III → IV → I).

Final Conceptual Answer: II → III → IV → I

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ALTERNATING_CURRENT_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Sequential steps in radio receiver tuning

questiontext.text:
The following steps describe the tuning mechanism of a radio set selecting a particular broadcasting station using a series LCR resonant circuit:

  1. The antenna intercepts electromagnetic broadcast signals transmitted simultaneously from multiple radio stations.
  2. The capacitance \(C\) of the tuning capacitor is continuously adjusted by the user.
  3. The incoming signals act as alternating voltage driving sources across the series tuning circuit at their respective frequencies.
  4. The natural resonant frequency \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\) of the tuning circuit becomes equal to the carrier frequency of the chosen station.
  5. The current amplitude corresponding to that specific station's frequency attains a sharp maximum (\(i_m = \frac{v_m}{R}\)), allowing that signal to be selectively extracted.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of the tuning process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A radio receiver uses the phenomenon of electrical resonance in an LCR circuit to selectively filter and amplify a single desired signal out of a broad spectrum of ambient electromagnetic carrier waves.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Mechanism
1. Signal Interception: The external antenna receives electromagnetic signals from numerous broadcasting stations simultaneously.
2. Driving the Circuit: The voltages induced in the antenna feed directly into the tuning circuit, driving it simultaneously across multiple frequencies.
3. Tuning Adjustment: In order to tune into a specific station, the listener rotates the tuning knob, which varies the capacitance \(C\) of the variable tuning capacitor inside the receiver.
4. Achieving Resonance: Changing \(C\) shifts the natural frequency \(\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}\) of the circuit until it precisely matches the broadcast frequency of the targeted station, causing the inductive and capacitive reactances to balance (\(X_L = X_C\)).
5. Peak Current Response: At this condition, the circuit impedance reaches its minimum value \(Z = R\), making the current amplitude for that particular carrier frequency dramatically larger than for all other non-resonant frequencies.

Step 3: Final Sequence
The correct operational order proceeds from antenna interception, to driving the circuit with mixed signals, adjusting the tuning capacitor, achieving frequency equality at resonance, and finally maximizing the current amplitude of the selected broadcast (I → III → II → IV → V).

Final Conceptual Answer: I → III → II → IV → V

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ALTERNATING_CURRENT_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Chronological progression in purely inductive circuit

questiontext.text:
An alternating voltage \(v(t) = v_m \sin(\omega t)\) is applied across an ideal, pure inductor of inductance \(L\). Consider the following physical events occurring during the first half-cycle of the applied voltage, in the interval \(0 \le \omega t \le \pi\):

  1. The instantaneous rate of energy absorption (instantaneous power supplied to the inductor) reaches its maximum negative value \(p_L = -\frac{v_m i_m}{2}\).
  2. The applied alternating voltage \(v(t)\) crosses zero while increasing in the positive direction.
  3. The instantaneous current \(i(t)\) in the inductor passes through zero and becomes positive.
  4. The applied alternating voltage \(v(t)\) reaches its first positive maximum value \(+v_m\).
  5. The instantaneous current \(i(t)\) reaches its first positive maximum value \(+i_m\).

Which of the following represents the strictly chronological sequence of these events from \(\omega t = 0\) to \(\omega t = \pi\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Applied voltage: \(v(t) = v_m \sin(\omega t)\).
Pure inductor of inductance \(L\).
Interval under consideration: \(0 \le \omega t \le \pi\).
The instantaneous current is \(i(t) = i_m \sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -i_m \cos(\omega t)\), where \(i_m = \frac{v_m}{\omega L}\).
The instantaneous power supplied to the inductor is \(p_L(t) = v(t) i(t) = v_m \sin(\omega t) \times [-i_m \cos(\omega t)] = -\frac{v_m i_m}{2} \sin(2\omega t)\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Time progresses continuously from \(\omega t = 0\) to \(\omega t = \pi\).
Phasors rotate counterclockwise with angular frequency \(\omega\).
A quantity's value and sign are directly determined by substituting the phase angle \(\omega t\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Voltage: \(v(\omega t) = v_m \sin(\omega t)\).
2. Current: \(i(\omega t) = -i_m \cos(\omega t)\).
3. Power: \(p_L(\omega t) = -\frac{v_m i_m}{2} \sin(2\omega t)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Chronological Evaluation
Let us determine the exact phase angle \(\omega t\) for each of the five events:
1. Event II: Applied voltage \(v(t)\) crosses zero with a positive slope (\(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} > 0\)). Since \(v(t) = v_m \sin(\omega t)\), this occurs at \(\omega t = 0\).
2. Event I: Instantaneous power \(p_L = -\frac{v_m i_m}{2}\sin(2\omega t)\) reaches its peak negative value \(-\frac{v_m i_m}{2}\) when \(\sin(2\omega t) = +1\). This requires \(2\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\), which gives \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{4}\).
3. Events III and IV: At \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\):
- Voltage reaches its maximum positive value: \(v\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = v_m \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = +v_m\) (Event IV).
- Current passes through zero: \(i\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -i_m \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0\), transitioning from negative to positive values (Event III).
Events III and IV occur simultaneously at \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
4. Event V: Current reaches its positive maximum value: \(i(\omega t) = -i_m \cos(\omega t) = +i_m\). This requires \(\cos(\omega t) = -1\), which occurs at \(\omega t = \pi\).
Ordering the unique timestamps:
- \(\omega t = 0\): Event II
- \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{4}\): Event I
- \(\omega t = \frac{\pi}{2}\): Events III and IV
- \(\omega t = \pi\): Event V
Between Events III and IV which occur at the exact same instant, the sequence is expressed as II → I → IV → III → V (or with III and IV co-occurring at \(\pi/2\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The chronological phases are verified: \(\omega t = 0\) (voltage crosses zero), \(\omega t = \pi/4\) (power reaches negative peak), \(\omega t = \pi/2\) (voltage reaches maximum positive while current passes through zero), and \(\omega t = \pi\) (current reaches maximum positive).
The correct chronological sequence is: II → I → IV → III → V.

Final Conceptual Answer: II → I → IV → III → V

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q01 - Advantage of alternating voltage in power transmission

questiontext.text: What is the primary advantage of alternating voltage over direct voltage in large-scale electrical power systems?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alternating voltage (ac voltage) displays simple harmonic time dependence and induces time-varying magnetic flux in magnetic cores.

Step 2: Evaluation
Transformers operate on the principle of mutual induction under a time-varying magnetic flux. Direct voltage (dc) produces a steady magnetic field, preventing transformer operation without complex switching.

Step 3: Application
Using transformers, ac voltages can be stepped up efficiently to very high voltages at generating stations. This minimizes the line current and drastically cuts down \(I^2R\) Joule heating losses during long-distance transmission, and can then be stepped down safely near consumer points.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decisive advantage is that alternating voltages can be converted easily and efficiently between different levels by means of transformers for economical transmission.

Final Answer: It can be stepped up or down efficiently using transformers for economical long-distance transmission.

answer.text: It maintains a constant magnitude and unidirectional flow of charge carriers.
It can be stepped up or down efficiently using transformers for economical long-distance transmission.
It eliminates all Joule heating losses in electrical transmission lines.
It allows storage of electrical energy in chemical batteries directly without conversion.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q02 - Average value of alternating current over one full cycle

questiontext.text: For a sinusoidal alternating current \(i = i_m \sin \omega t\), the sum of instantaneous current values over one complete cycle is zero. What is the average current over a complete cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The average value of a time-dependent periodic function \(F(t)\) over a time period \(T\) is defined as \(\langle F(t) \rangle = \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T F(t) \, \mathrm{d}t\).

Step 2: Evaluation
For a sinusoidal current \(i(t) = i_m \sin(\omega t)\), the waveform has identical positive and negative half-cycles. The area under the curve during the positive half-cycle from \(0\) to \(T/2\) is exactly cancelled by the area under the negative half-cycle from \(T/2\) to \(T\).

Step 3: Application
Evaluating the integral gives \(\int_0^T \sin(\omega t)\,\mathrm{d}t = \left[-\frac{\cos(\omega t)}{\omega}\right]_0^T = -\frac{1}{\omega}[\cos(2\pi) - \cos(0)] = 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The average current of a sinusoidal alternating current over one complete cycle is identically zero.

Final Answer: Zero

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q03 - Phase relation across pure resistor in ac circuit

questiontext.text: When a sinusoidal alternating voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\) is applied across a pure ohmic resistor \(R\), what is the phase relationship between the applied voltage and the resulting current?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Ohm's law applied to an instantaneous alternating circuit, the current through a pure resistor of resistance \(R\) is given by \(i = \frac{v}{R}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Substituting the applied voltage \(v = v_m \sin(\omega t)\) yields \(i = \frac{v_m}{R} \sin(\omega t) = i_m \sin(\omega t)\), where \(i_m = \frac{v_m}{R}\).

Step 3: Application
Both \(v(t)\) and \(i(t)\) vary as \(\sin(\omega t)\) without any angular offset. Consequently, they attain their zero crossings, positive peaks, and negative peaks at the exact same moments in time.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In a purely resistive alternating circuit, the phase difference between voltage and current is zero, meaning they are completely in phase.

Final Answer: The voltage and current are in phase with each other.

answer.text: The voltage and current are in opposite phase with a difference of \(\pi\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q04 - Peak voltage calculation from root mean square value

questiontext.text: A household ac mains supply has an effective (rms) voltage of \(220\text{ V}\). What is the peak value (amplitude) of this alternating voltage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Root-mean-square voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The voltage varies sinusoidally as \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\), where \(v_m\) represents the peak voltage.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The relationship between rms voltage \(V\) and peak voltage \(v_m\) for a sinusoidal wave is \(V = \frac{v_m}{\sqrt{2}}\), which gives \(v_m = \sqrt{2} V\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given numerical value into the formula:
\[ v_m = \sqrt{2} \times 220\text{ V} \approx 1.414 \times 220\text{ V} = 311.08\text{ V} \approx 311\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The peak voltage must exceed the rms value by a factor of approximately \(1.414\). The calculation gives \(311\text{ V}\).

Final Answer: \(311\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q05 - Average power dissipation in a purely resistive circuit

questiontext.text: An alternating current \(i = i_m \sin \omega t\) passes through a pure resistor of resistance \(R\). Even though the average current over a complete cycle is zero, electrical energy is dissipated. Why does net power dissipation occur?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to Joule's law of heating, the instantaneous power dissipated in a resistor of resistance \(R\) carrying instantaneous current \(i\) is given by \(p = i^2 R\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the term \(i^2\) involves the square of the instantaneous current, its value is always greater than or equal to zero, regardless of whether \(i\) is positive or negative.

Step 3: Application
Over one complete cycle, the average of \(\sin^2(\omega t)\) is \(\langle \sin^2(\omega t) \rangle = \frac{1}{2}\). Hence, the average power dissipated is \(\overline{p} = \frac{1}{2} i_m^2 R = I^2 R > 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Power is dissipated as heat because heating depends on \(i^2\) rather than \(i\), ensuring that electrical energy dissipation is continuous and cumulative throughout both half-cycles.

Final Answer: Joule heating depends on the square of current, \(i^2R\), which remains strictly non-negative at all instants.

answer.text: The resistance of the resistor changes sign in accordance with the current alternating direction.
Joule heating depends directly on \(i\), and the positive half-cycle produces more heat than the negative half-cycle.
The average power is non-zero because the frequency of the applied alternating voltage is non-zero.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q06 - Resistance and rms current of a light bulb

questiontext.text: An incandescent electric bulb is rated at \(100\text{ W}\) for a \(220\text{ V}\) ac supply. What are the resistance of the bulb and the rms current flowing through it?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Power rating \(P = 100\text{ W}\), supply rms voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The filament behaves as a pure ohmic resistance at its operating temperature.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For an ac circuit with rms values, average power is given by \(P = \frac{V^2}{R} = V I\), so \(R = \frac{V^2}{P}\) and \(I = \frac{P}{V}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate resistance:
\[ R = \frac{(220\text{ V})^2}{100\text{ W}} = \frac{48400}{100} = 484\ \Omega \]
Calculate rms current:
\[ I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{100\text{ W}}{220\text{ V}} = \frac{5}{11}\text{ A} \approx 0.454\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking with \(I^2 R\): \((0.4545)^2 \times 484 \approx 0.2066 \times 484 \approx 100\text{ W}\). Thus, \(R = 484\ \Omega\) and \(I = 0.454\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(R = 484\ \Omega\) and \(I = 0.454\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q07 - Peak current calculation from root mean square current

questiontext.text: The root-mean-square value of current in an alternating current circuit is \(10\text{ A}\). What is the peak value of this current?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
RMS current \(I = 10\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Sinusoidal alternating waveform is assumed.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The relation between peak current \(i_m\) and rms current \(I\) is \(I = \frac{i_m}{\sqrt{2}}\), which yields \(i_m = \sqrt{2} I\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given value:
\[ i_m = \sqrt{2} \times 10\text{ A} \approx 1.4142 \times 10\text{ A} = 14.14\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The peak current is strictly greater than the rms current by the factor \(\sqrt{2}\). The resulting peak current is \(14.14\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(14.14\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q08 - Peak voltage of standard domestic mains supply

questiontext.text: The ac voltage across the terminals of a domestic wall socket is specified as \(240\text{ V}\). What is the amplitude (peak value) of this alternating voltage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Specified ac terminal voltage \(V = 240\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Unless specified otherwise, any given voltage in an ac circuit refers to the root-mean-square (rms) value.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The peak voltage \(v_m\) is related to the rms voltage \(V\) by \(v_m = \sqrt{2} V\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Multiply the rms value by \(\sqrt{2}\):
\[ v_m = \sqrt{2} \times 240\text{ V} \approx 1.4142 \times 240\text{ V} \approx 339.4\text{ V} \approx 340\text{ V} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying \(240\) by \(1.414\) gives \(339.4\text{ V}\), rounding to \(340\text{ V}\).

Final Answer: \(340\text{ V}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q09 - Definition of the ampere for alternating current

questiontext.text: Why cannot the unit 'ampere' for alternating current be derived from the mutual magnetic attraction between two parallel current-carrying conductors as it is for direct current?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The magnetic force per unit length between two parallel conductors depends directly on the product of the currents in each conductor: \(F/L \propto i_1(t) i_2(t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
If the conductors carry ac current with a phase difference or if defined externally, the magnetic attraction oscillates. More importantly, an ac current changes direction every half-cycle, so any force derived directly from linear magnetic effects averages to zero over time.

Step 3: Application
Consequently, the ac ampere is defined using Joule heating—a property proportional to \(i^2(t)\), which is independent of the current's direction. One ac ampere (rms) produces the same average heating effect as one ampere of steady dc under identical conditions.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The magnetic attraction averages to zero due to continuous directional reversal, necessitating a direction-independent thermal definition.

Final Answer: Because an alternating current periodically reverses direction, making the time-average of the magnetic force between parallel wires zero.

answer.text: Because the magnetic permeability of the surrounding space oscillates between positive and negative values.
Because an alternating current periodically reverses direction, making the time-average of the magnetic force between parallel wires zero.
Because the mutual magnetic force between parallel ac conductors is always repulsive rather than attractive.
Because alternating currents do not establish any magnetic fields around the conductors.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q10 - Phase relationship in a purely inductive circuit

questiontext.text: When a purely inductive circuit with zero winding resistance is connected across a sinusoidal alternating voltage source, what is the phase difference between the current and the voltage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Applying Kirchhoff's loop rule to a pure inductor connected across an ac voltage source \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\) yields \(v - L \frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Integrating \(\frac{\mathrm{d}i}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{v_m}{L} \sin \omega t\) with respect to time gives \(i = -\frac{v_m}{\omega L} \cos \omega t\).

Step 3: Application
Using the trigonometric identity \(-\cos \omega t = \sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), the current is expressed as \(i = i_m \sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The current waveform reaches its peaks and zero crossings one-quarter of a period (\(T/4\)) later than the voltage waveform, meaning the current lags the voltage by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

Final Answer: The current lags behind the voltage by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians.

answer.text: The current lags behind the voltage by \(\pi\) radians.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q11 - Time period and frequency of Indian domestic supply

questiontext.text: The domestic electric supply in India operates at a standard frequency of \(50\text{ Hz}\). How much time elapses between two consecutive reversals of the current direction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency of domestic alternating supply \(\nu = 50\text{ Hz}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A full cycle corresponds to a period \(T = \frac{1}{\nu}\). In each cycle, the sinusoidal current changes direction twice (every half-cycle).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The time period of one complete oscillation is \(T = \frac{1}{\nu}\). The interval between two consecutive reversals of direction is equal to half a period, \(\Delta t = \frac{T}{2} = \frac{1}{2\nu}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the time period:
\[ T = \frac{1}{50\text{ s}^{-1}} = 0.02\text{ s} = 20\text{ ms} \]
Calculate the time between direction reversals:
\[ \Delta t = \frac{T}{2} = \frac{20\text{ ms}}{2} = 10\text{ ms} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
In one second there are \(50\) complete cycles, corresponding to \(100\) reversals of current direction. The time between consecutive reversals is \(\frac{1}{100}\text{ s} = 0.01\text{ s} = 10\text{ ms}\).

Final Answer: \(10\text{ ms}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q12 - Nature of physical quantities represented by phasors

questiontext.text: In alternating current circuit analysis, voltages and currents are represented geometrically as rotating vectors called phasors. Which statement correctly characterizes these physical quantities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electric potential difference (voltage) and electric current do not possess spatial orientation or direction in space; they are scalar quantities governed by algebraic conservation laws.

Step 2: Evaluation
When two harmonically varying scalar quantities of the same frequency are added, their sum depends on their amplitudes and phase differences in a manner mathematically identical to the addition of two vectors in a two-dimensional plane.

Step 3: Application
Phasors are defined as fictitious vectors rotating about the origin at angular speed \(\omega\). The projections of these phasors onto the vertical axis represent the instantaneous scalar values \(v_m \sin \omega t\) and \(i_m \sin \omega t\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Voltages and currents are true scalars whose harmonic mathematical addition is conveniently handled by treating them as projections of rotating vectors.

Final Answer: Voltages and currents are scalar quantities, but their harmonically varying phases and amplitudes combine mathematically like rotating vectors.

answer.text: Voltages and currents are pseudoscalars whose dot products yield magnetic flux.
Voltages and currents are scalar quantities, but their harmonically varying phases and amplitudes combine mathematically like rotating vectors.
Phasors are stationary vectors whose magnitude increases linearly with time.
Voltages and currents are true physical vectors that point in spatial directions inside the wire.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q13 - Physical interpretation of the phasor diagram projection

questiontext.text: In a phasor diagram representing an alternating voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\), what does the projection of the rotating phasor \(\mathbf{V}\) onto the vertical axis represent at any instant \(t\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A phasor \(\mathbf{V}\) is a vector of constant length equal to the peak value \(v_m\), rotating counterclockwise at constant angular velocity \(\omega\) starting from the horizontal axis at \(t = 0\).

Step 2: Evaluation
At time \(t\), the angle made by \(\mathbf{V}\) with the horizontal reference axis is \(\theta = \omega t\).

Step 3: Application
The vertical component (projection onto the vertical axis) of a vector of magnitude \(v_m\) inclined at an angle \(\omega t\) is given by \(v_m \sin \omega t\). This expression is precisely the instantaneous voltage \(v(t)\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The vertical projection of the voltage phasor at any instant represents the instantaneous value of the alternating voltage.

Final Answer: The instantaneous value of the alternating voltage at that time.

answer.text: The total power dissipated in the circuit up to that time.
The root-mean-square value of the alternating voltage.
The peak amplitude \(v_m\) of the oscillating voltage.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q14 - Average power consumed by a pure inductor

questiontext.text: What is the net average power supplied by an alternating voltage source to a purely inductive circuit over one complete cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The instantaneous power supplied to an inductor carrying current \(i = i_m \sin\left(\omega t - \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -i_m \cos \omega t\) under applied voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\) is \(p_L = v i = -i_m v_m \sin \omega t \cos \omega t = -\frac{i_m v_m}{2} \sin(2\omega t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The average power over a complete cycle is \(P_L = \langle p_L \rangle = -\frac{i_m v_m}{2} \langle \sin(2\omega t) \rangle\).

Step 3: Application
The function \(\sin(2\omega t)\) oscillates symmetrically between \(+1\) and \(-1\) over a period \(T\), giving an average value of identically zero: \(\langle \sin(2\omega t) \rangle = 0\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Energy stored in the magnetic field during one quarter of a cycle is fully returned to the source during the next quarter; therefore, the net average power absorbed over a complete cycle is zero.

Final Answer: Zero

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q15 - Phase relation across pure capacitor in ac circuit

questiontext.text: An alternating voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\) is applied across a pure capacitor of capacitance \(C\). What is the phase relationship of the alternating current relative to the voltage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The instantaneous charge on a capacitor is \(q(t) = C v(t) = C v_m \sin(\omega t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The instantaneous current is the time derivative of charge: \(i = \frac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega C v_m \cos(\omega t)\).

Step 3: Application
Using the trigonometric identity \(\cos(\omega t) = \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), the current becomes \(i = i_m \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The current reaches its maximum value one-fourth of a cycle (\(T/4\)) earlier than the voltage, demonstrating that the current leads the voltage by \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

Final Answer: The current leads the voltage by a phase angle of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

answer.text: The current lags behind the voltage by a phase angle of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
The current leads the voltage by a phase angle of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
The current leads the voltage by a phase angle of \(\pi\).
The current and voltage oscillate exactly in phase.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q16 - Inductive reactance and rms current of pure inductor

questiontext.text: A pure inductor of self-inductance \(25.0\text{ mH}\) is connected to a \(220\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) ac source. What are the inductive reactance of the inductor and the rms current in the circuit? (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Self-inductance \(L = 25.0\text{ mH} = 25.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}\), rms voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\), frequency \(\nu = 50\text{ Hz}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Winding resistance is negligible (pure inductor).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The inductive reactance is \(X_L = \omega L = 2 \pi \nu L\). The rms current is given by Ohm's law analogue: \(I = \frac{V}{X_L}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(X_L\):
\[ X_L = 2 \times 3.14 \times 50\text{ s}^{-1} \times 25.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H} = 314 \times 0.025\ \Omega = 7.85\ \Omega \]
Calculate rms current \(I\):
\[ I = \frac{220\text{ V}}{7.85\ \Omega} \approx 28.025\text{ A} \approx 28\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The inductive reactance is \(7.85\ \Omega\) and the rms current is \(28\text{ A}\), which matches NCERT Example 7.2.

Final Answer: \(X_L = 7.85\ \Omega\) and \(I = 28\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q17 - Frequency dependence of inductive reactance and current

questiontext.text: An alternating voltage of constant amplitude is applied across an inductor of fixed self-inductance. If the operating frequency of the source is doubled, how do the inductive reactance and the circuit current change?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Inductive reactance represents the opposition offered by an inductor to alternating current and is given by \(X_L = \omega L = 2 \pi \nu L\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Since \(X_L\) is directly proportional to the frequency \(\nu\), doubling the frequency (\(\nu' = 2\nu\)) doubles the inductive reactance: \(X_L' = 2 X_L\).

Step 3: Application
The amplitude of current through the inductor is \(i_m = \frac{v_m}{X_L}\). With constant voltage amplitude \(v_m\), doubling the reactance reduces the current by half: \(i_m' = \frac{v_m}{2 X_L} = \frac{i_m}{2}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Doubling the alternating source frequency causes the inductive reactance to double and the resulting current to be halved.

Final Answer: The inductive reactance is doubled and the current is halved.

answer.text: The inductive reactance is doubled and the current is halved.
The inductive reactance is halved and the current is doubled.
Both the inductive reactance and the current are doubled.
The inductive reactance is quadrupled and the current is halved.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q18 - Effect of inserting iron core into inductor

questiontext.text: An electric bulb and an air-cored open inductor are connected in series across an ac source. When a soft iron rod is inserted into the interior of the inductor coil, what happens to the brightness of the bulb?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The self-inductance \(L\) of a solenoid is directly proportional to the relative magnetic permeability \(\mu_r\) of its core material: \(L = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_r N^2 A}{l}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Inserting a soft iron rod (\(\mu_r \gg 1\)) into the coil significantly increases its self-inductance \(L\). Consequently, the inductive reactance \(X_L = \omega L\) increases substantially.

Step 3: Application
The circuit impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2}\) increases, which decreases the current \(I = \frac{V}{Z}\) flowing through the bulb. Moreover, a larger fraction of the source voltage drops across the inductor, leaving less potential across the bulb filament.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because the circuit current and filament voltage decrease, the power dissipated in the bulb decreases, causing its glow to diminish.

Final Answer: The brightness of the bulb decreases.

answer.text: The brightness of the bulb remains completely unchanged.
The bulb glows brighter initially and then turns off permanently.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q19 - Root mean square current in inductive circuit

questiontext.text: A \(44\text{ mH}\) inductor is connected to a \(220\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) ac supply. Determine the rms value of the alternating current in the circuit. (Take \(\pi = \frac{22}{7}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Self-inductance \(L = 44\text{ mH} = 44 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}\), supply voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\), frequency \(\nu = 50\text{ Hz}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coil has negligible resistance and represents an ideal pure inductor.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Inductive reactance is \(X_L = 2 \pi \nu L\). The rms current is \(I = \frac{V}{X_L}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate inductive reactance \(X_L\):
\[ X_L = 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 50 \times 44 \times 10^{-3} = \frac{44 \times 50 \times 44 \times 10^{-3}}{7} = \frac{96.8}{7} \approx 13.83\ \Omega \]
Calculate the rms current \(I\):
\[ I = \frac{220\text{ V}}{13.83\ \Omega} \approx 15.91\text{ A} \approx 15.9\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
With \(X_L \approx 13.8\ \Omega\), dividing \(220\) by \(13.8\) gives \(15.9\text{ A}\). This conforms with standard exercise solutions.

Final Answer: \(15.9\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q20 - Dimensions and units of inductive and capacitive reactance

questiontext.text: What are the SI unit and dimensional formula of inductive reactance \(X_L\) and capacitive reactance \(X_C\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both inductive reactance \(X_L = \omega L\) and capacitive reactance \(X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}\) represent opposition to alternating current, defined as the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude: \(X = \frac{V}{I}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because reactance is the ratio of potential difference to current, its SI unit is the ohm (\(\Omega\)), identical to that of electrical resistance.

Step 3: Application
Electric potential has dimensions \([V] = \frac{[\text{Work}]}{[\text{Charge}]} = \frac{\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-2}}{\text{A}\ \text{T}} = [\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-3}\ \text{A}^{-1}]\). Dividing by current \([\text{A}]\) gives \([X] = \frac{[\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-3}\ \text{A}^{-1}]}{[\text{A}]} = [\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-3}\ \text{A}^{-2}]\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both inductive and capacitive reactance have the unit ohm (\(\Omega\)) and dimensional formula \([\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-3}\ \text{A}^{-2}]\).

Final Answer: Unit: \(\text{ohm}\ (\Omega)\); Dimensions: \([\text{M}\ \text{L}^2\ \text{T}^{-3}\ \text{A}^{-2}]\) for both.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q21 - Capacitor response to dc versus ac voltage sources

questiontext.text: A lamp is connected in series with a capacitor. When connected across a dc source, the lamp does not glow, but when connected across an ac source, it shines steadily. What explains this difference?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Capacitive reactance is given by \(X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi \nu C}\), where \(\nu\) is the frequency of the electrical source.

Step 2: Evaluation
For a direct current (dc) source, frequency \(\nu = 0\), which yields an infinite capacitive reactance (\(X_C \to \infty\)). The capacitor charges rapidly to the supply voltage and completely halts the flow of direct current.

Step 3: Application
For an alternating current (ac) source, frequency \(\nu > 0\), yielding a finite reactance \(X_C\). The capacitor plates undergo continuous charging and discharging as polarity reverses every half-cycle, sustaining an alternating displacement and conduction current that lights the lamp.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
A capacitor blocks steady dc after an initial transient but permits ac to flow by offering a finite reactance.

Final Answer: The capacitor blocks dc once charged as its reactance is infinite for zero frequency, but provides finite reactance to ac by alternating charging and discharging.

answer.text: The ac source delivers higher voltage than the dc source regardless of source rating.
The capacitor blocks dc once charged as its reactance is infinite for zero frequency, but provides finite reactance to ac by alternating charging and discharging.
The capacitor dissipates more thermal energy in a dc circuit than in an ac circuit.
The dielectric material inside the capacitor conducts steady direct current but acts as an insulator for alternating current.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q22 - Capacitive reactance of capacitor at mains frequency

questiontext.text: A \(15.0\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is connected across a \(220\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) alternating supply. What is the capacitive reactance of the capacitor? (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance \(C = 15.0\ \mu\text{F} = 15.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), frequency \(\nu = 50\text{ Hz}\), rms voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The capacitor is ideal with zero dielectric losses and negligible lead resistance.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Capacitive reactance is given by \(X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2 \pi \nu C}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given numerical parameters into the expression:
\[ X_C = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.14 \times 50\text{ s}^{-1} \times 15.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}} = \frac{1}{314 \times 15.0 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{4.71 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 212.3\ \Omega \]
Rounding to three significant figures yields \(212\ \Omega\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The value of \(X_C \approx 212\ \Omega\) perfectly reproduces Example 7.4 of the textbook.

Final Answer: \(212\ \Omega\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q23 - Peak current in pure capacitive ac circuit

questiontext.text: A \(15.0\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is connected to a \(220\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) ac source. Given that its capacitive reactance is \(212\ \Omega\), what is the peak current flowing in the circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
RMS voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\), capacitive reactance \(X_C = 212\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The voltage varies sinusoidally, and the circuit is purely capacitive.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The rms current is \(I = \frac{V}{X_C}\), and the peak current is \(i_m = \sqrt{2} I\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the rms current:
\[ I = \frac{220\text{ V}}{212\ \Omega} \approx 1.0377\text{ A} \approx 1.04\text{ A} \]
Calculate the peak current:
\[ i_m = \sqrt{2} \times I = 1.4142 \times 1.0377\text{ A} \approx 1.4675\text{ A} \approx 1.47\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The peak current exceeds the rms current by the factor \(\sqrt{2}\). The calculated value is \(1.47\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(1.47\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q24 - Effect of doubling frequency on capacitive circuit

questiontext.text: A capacitor is connected to an ac voltage generator of variable frequency. If the frequency of the generator is doubled while maintaining its output voltage amplitude constant, what happens to the capacitive reactance and the current amplitude?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to the frequency: \(X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi \nu C}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
When the source frequency is doubled (\(\nu' = 2\nu\)), the new reactance becomes \(X_C' = \frac{1}{2\pi (2\nu) C} = \frac{X_C}{2}\). Thus, the capacitive reactance is halved.

Step 3: Application
The current amplitude is given by \(i_m = \frac{v_m}{X_C}\). With \(v_m\) held constant, \(i_m' = \frac{v_m}{X_C/2} = 2 \left(\frac{v_m}{X_C}\right) = 2 i_m\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Doubling the frequency halves the opposition offered by the capacitor, causing the current amplitude to double.

Final Answer: The capacitive reactance is halved and the current amplitude is doubled.

answer.text: Both the capacitive reactance and the current amplitude are doubled.
The capacitive reactance is doubled and the current amplitude is halved.
Both the capacitive reactance and the current amplitude are halved.
The capacitive reactance is halved and the current amplitude is doubled.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q25 - Average power absorption of an ideal capacitor

questiontext.text: Why is the average electrical power absorbed by an ideal capacitor over one complete cycle of alternating voltage equal to zero?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The instantaneous power supplied to a capacitor is \(p_C = v i = [v_m \sin \omega t] [i_m \cos \omega t] = \frac{v_m i_m}{2} \sin(2\omega t)\).

Step 2: Evaluation
The average power over one period \(T\) is \(P_C = \frac{v_m i_m}{2} \langle \sin(2\omega t) \rangle\). Over a complete cycle, the time average \(\langle \sin(2\omega t) \rangle\) is zero.

Step 3: Application
Physically, during the first quarter-cycle as voltage increases, energy is taken from the source to build an electric field (\(U = \frac{1}{2} C v^2\)). During the second quarter-cycle as voltage falls to zero, the electric field collapses and this energy is fully returned to the ac source.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Because the net exchange of energy over any full cycle is zero, the average power dissipated is zero.

Final Answer: The capacitor stores electrostatic energy during charging and fully returns it to the source during discharging every quarter-cycle.

answer.text: Because the voltage across the capacitor remains constant while current alternates.
The capacitor stores electrostatic energy during charging and fully returns it to the source during discharging every quarter-cycle.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q26 - Alternating current in capacitive circuit calculation

questiontext.text: A \(60\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is connected to a \(110\text{ V}\), \(60\text{ Hz}\) ac supply. Determine the rms value of the current in the circuit. (Take \(\pi = 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance \(C = 60\ \mu\text{F} = 60 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}\), rms voltage \(V = 110\text{ V}\), frequency \(\nu = 60\text{ Hz}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Capacitor is purely reactive with zero resistance.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Capacitive reactance is \(X_C = \frac{1}{2\pi \nu C}\). The rms current is \(I = \frac{V}{X_C} = 2\pi \nu C V\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(X_C\):
\[ X_C = \frac{1}{2 \times 3.14 \times 60 \times 60 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{1}{0.022608} \approx 44.23\ \Omega \]
Calculate rms current \(I\):
\[ I = \frac{110\text{ V}}{44.23\ \Omega} \approx 2.487\text{ A} \approx 2.49\text{ A} \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Direct substitution into \(I = 2\pi \nu C V = 2 \times 3.1416 \times 60 \times 60 \times 10^{-6} \times 110 = 2.488\text{ A} \approx 2.49\text{ A}\).

Final Answer: \(2.49\text{ A}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q27 - Series LCR circuit impedance formula and behavior

questiontext.text: In a series LCR circuit driven by an ac voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\), what is the impedance \(Z\) of the circuit, and under what condition does the current lead the applied voltage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a series LCR circuit, the voltage phasors are \(\mathbf{V}_R\) along \(\mathbf{I}\), \(\mathbf{V}_L\) leading \(\mathbf{I}\) by \(\pi/2\), and \(\mathbf{V}_C\) lagging \(\mathbf{I}\) by \(\pi/2\).

Step 2: Evaluation
Because \(\mathbf{V}_L\) and \(\mathbf{V}_C\) act along the same line in opposite directions, the net reactive voltage is \(|v_{Cm} - v_{Lm}| = i_m |X_C - X_L|\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to the right triangle yields \(v_m = i_m \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}\).

Step 3: Application
Thus, impedance is \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}\). The phase angle is \(\tan \phi = \frac{X_C - X_L}{R}\). When \(X_C > X_L\), \(\phi > 0\), meaning the circuit is predominantly capacitive and current leads the source voltage.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The impedance is \(\sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}\) and the current leads the voltage when \(X_C > X_L\).

Final Answer: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}\), and current leads voltage when \(X_C > X_L\).

answer.text: \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + X_L^2 + X_C^2}\), and current leads voltage when \(X_L = X_C\).
\(Z = \sqrt{R^2 - (X_L - X_C)^2}\), and current leads voltage when \(X_L > X_C\).
\(Z = R + X_L + X_C\), and current leads voltage when \(X_L > X_C\).
\(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_C - X_L)^2}\), and current leads voltage when \(X_C > X_L\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q28 - Non-algebraic addition of voltages in series RC circuit

questiontext.text: In a series RC circuit connected to a \(220\text{ V}\), \(50\text{ Hz}\) source, the rms voltage across the resistor is \(V_R = 151\text{ V}\) and across the capacitor is \(V_C = 160.3\text{ V}\). Why does their algebraic sum (\(311.3\text{ V}\)) exceed the source voltage (\(220\text{ V}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
RMS voltages: \(V_R = 151\text{ V}\), \(V_C = 160.3\text{ V}\), source voltage \(V = 220\text{ V}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The current phasor is taken as the reference; \(V_R\) is in phase with current, whereas \(V_C\) lags current by \(90^\circ\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Because the potential differences are mutually perpendicular phasors, the total rms voltage is \(V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the phasor resultant:
\[ V = \sqrt{(151)^2 + (160.3)^2} = \sqrt{22801 + 25696.09} = \sqrt{48497.09} \approx 220.2\text{ V} \approx 220\text{ V} \]
The algebraic sum \(151 + 160.3 = 311.3\text{ V}\) fails because it assumes zero phase difference.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Vectorial addition correctly accounts for the \(90^\circ\) phase difference and matches the source voltage of \(220\text{ V}\).

Final Answer: The voltages across the resistor and capacitor are out of phase by \(90^\circ\) and must be added vectorially: \(\sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2} = 220\text{ V}\).

answer.text: The voltmeter readings represent instantaneous peak values rather than rms quantities.
The voltages across the resistor and capacitor are out of phase by \(90^\circ\) and must be added vectorially: \(\sqrt{V_R^2 + V_C^2} = 220\text{ V}\).
Ohm's law does not hold for circuits containing capacitive reactance.
Energy is created by electrostatic oscillations inside the dielectric medium.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q29 - Calculation of impedance for series LCR circuit

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit has a resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\), an inductive reactance \(X_L = 8\ \Omega\), and a capacitive reactance \(X_C = 4\ \Omega\). What is the total impedance of the circuit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Resistance \(R = 3\ \Omega\), inductive reactance \(X_L = 8\ \Omega\), capacitive reactance \(X_C = 4\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The components are connected in series; net reactance is \(X = |X_L - X_C|\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The impedance of a series LCR circuit is given by \(Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the net reactance:
\[ X_L - X_C = 8\ \Omega - 4\ \Omega = 4\ \Omega \]
Calculate the impedance:
\[ Z = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\ \Omega \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The calculation forms a standard 3-4-5 right triangle. The resulting impedance is \(5\ \Omega\).

Final Answer: \(5\ \Omega\)

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CH07_MCQ_Q30 - Phase difference between current and voltage in LCR

questiontext.text: A series LCR circuit has \(R = 3\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 8\ \Omega\), and \(X_C = 4\ \Omega\). What is the phase difference \(\phi\) of the current relative to the applied voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(R = 3\ \Omega\), \(X_L = 8\ \Omega\), \(X_C = 4\ \Omega\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
With source voltage \(v = v_m \sin \omega t\), current is written as \(i = i_m \sin(\omega t + \phi)\), where \(\tan \phi = \frac{X_C - X_L}{R}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The phase angle is \(\tan \phi = \frac{X_C - X_L}{R}\). If \(\phi < 0\), the current lags behind the voltage.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the reactive values:
\[ \tan \phi = \frac{4 - 8}{3} = -\frac{4}{3} \approx -1.333 \]
Taking the arctangent:
\[ \phi = \tan^{-1}\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right) \approx -53.1^\circ \]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(X_L > X_C\), the circuit is predominantly inductive, so the current must lag the voltage. The phase angle is \(-53.1^\circ\).

Final Answer: \(\phi = -53.1^\circ\), meaning the current lags behind the applied voltage.
